parts.latex: A box contains $m$ yellow balls and 20 black balls. If a ball is randomly drawn from the box, then the probability of drawing a yellow ball is $\dfrac{1}{5}$. What is the value of $m$?

solutions.latex:
The probability of a yellow ball is the number of yellow balls over the total number of balls.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{m}{m+20} &= \dfrac{1}{5} \\ 5m &= m+20 \\ 4m &= 20 \\ m &= 5 \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: normal distribution curve, shaded between x = 25 and x = 145, dashed line at the mean

solutions.latex:
Approximately $99.7\%$ of the area lies within $3$ standard deviations of the mean, so $x=25$ and $x=145$ are $\mu-3\sigma$ and $\mu+3\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= \dfrac{25+145}{2} \\ &= 85 \\ 3\sigma &= 145-85 \\ &= 60 \\ \sigma &= 20 \\ \operatorname{Var}(X) &= \sigma^2 \\ &= 400 \end{aligned}$$
So the mean is $85$ and the variance is $400$.

parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=\sqrt{25-x^2}+\sqrt{x}$ ?

solutions.latex:
The square root $\sqrt{25-x^2}$ needs $25-x^2\ge 0$, so its domain is $[-5,5]$. The square root $\sqrt{x}$ needs $x\ge 0$, so its domain is $[0,\infty)$. Both must hold:
$$[-5,5]\cap[0,\infty)=[0,5]$$

parts.latex:
The cost \$$c$ of making a box of cookies is inversely proportional to the square of the number of boxes $n$ made.

Which of the following is a possible equation of the model?

solutions.latex:
$c$ is inversely proportional to $n^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} c &= \dfrac{k}{n^2} \\ cn^2 &= k \end{aligned}$$
Since $c$ and $n^2$ are positive, $k$ is positive, so $cn^2=10$ is possible and $cn^2=-10$ is not.

parts.latex:
Let $f'(x)=g'(x)-1$, where $f(0)=2$ and $g(0)=1$.

Which of the following is an expression for $f(x)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Integrate $f'(x)=g'(x)-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \int\big(g'(x)-1\big)\,dx \\ &= g(x)-x+c \end{aligned}$$
Use $f(0)=2$ and $g(0)=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= g(0)-0+c \\ 2 &= 1-0+c \\ c &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=g(x)-x+1$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $\dfrac{x^3}{\ln x}$ with respect to $x$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{\ln x}\right) &= \dfrac{3x^2\ln x-x^3\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{3x^2\ln x-x^2}{(\ln x)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the quotient rule with $u$, $v$, $u'$ and $v'$, or equivalent merit

1761.stem: The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=\dfrac{1}{2}n(3n+2)$.

parts.latex: Find the first three terms of the series.
Find an expression for the $n$th term of the series.

solutions.latex:
The first term is $T_1=S_1$, and each later term is $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$ (the sum of $n$ terms less the sum of $n-1$ terms).
$$\begin{aligned} S_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1)\big(3(1)+2\big)=\dfrac{5}{2} \\ S_2 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(2)\big(3(2)+2\big)=8 \\ S_3 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(3)\big(3(3)+2\big)=\dfrac{33}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T_1 &= S_1=\dfrac{5}{2} \\ T_2 &= S_2-S_1=8-\dfrac{5}{2}=\dfrac{11}{2} \\ T_3 &= S_3-S_2=\dfrac{33}{2}-8=\dfrac{17}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first three terms are $\dfrac{5}{2}$, $\dfrac{11}{2}$ and $\dfrac{17}{2}$.

From part (a), $a=\dfrac{5}{2}$ and $d=\dfrac{11}{2}-\dfrac{5}{2}=3$. Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= \dfrac{5}{2}+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\ &= \dfrac{5}{2}+3n-3 \\ &= 3n-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= \dfrac{1}{2}n(3n+2)-\dfrac{1}{2}(n-1)\big(3(n-1)+2\big) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\big[3n^2+2n-(n-1)(3n-1)\big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\big[3n^2+2n-(3n^2-4n+1)\big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(6n-1) \\ &= 3n-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=e^{\cos(\pi x)}$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{u}\right)=u'e^{u}$ with $u=\cos\pi x$:
$$y'=-\pi\sin\pi x\cdot e^{\cos\pi x}$$
At $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} m_T &= -\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot e^{\cos\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\pi(1)e^0 \\ &= -\pi \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent:
$$\begin{aligned} m_N &= -\dfrac{1}{m_T} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $y=e^{\cos\frac{\pi}{2}}=e^0=1$, so the point is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},1\right)$. The normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi}\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ \pi y-\pi &= x-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ 2x-2\pi y+2\pi-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Equivalently, $y=\dfrac{1}{\pi}x-\dfrac{1}{2\pi}+1$.
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator using $1-\cos^4\theta=\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)$ and $1-\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^4\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta\sin^2\theta &&(\text{cancel } 1+\cos^2\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\cdot\sin^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\sin\theta \\ &= \tan\theta\sin\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\tan\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$

solutions.latex:
Let $x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ be the angle to solve for; its range is found from the range of $x$, one operation per line.
$$\begin{aligned} -\pi &\le x\le\pi \\ -\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4} &\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4} &&(\text{add }\dfrac{\pi}{4}) \\ -\dfrac{3\pi}{4} &\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le\dfrac{5\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. Tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants, and $\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\pi=-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is outside the range, so
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= -\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the solutions for $x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, or equivalent merit

1766.stem:
Bill runs around a triangular shaped park, starting and ending at gate $A$. He runs 12 km from $A$ to $B$ on a bearing of $N29^{\circ}E$, then runs 20 km from $B$ to $C$ on a bearing of $S31^{\circ}E$. Lastly, he runs back to $A$.

\exfigure{382_q19_1}

figures.cap: triangular park ABC shaded, with north arrows at A, B and C

parts.latex: Find the exact area of the park.
Find the total distance Bill ran.

solutions.latex:
The north lines at $A$ and $B$ are parallel, so (alternate angles) $BA$ makes an angle of $29^\circ$ with the south line at $B$, and $BC$ makes $31^\circ$ with it on the other side.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ABC &= 29^\circ+31^\circ \\ &= 60^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 12\times 20\times\sin 60^\circ \\ &= 60\sqrt{3}\text{ km}^2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: The 'exact' answer is assessed in Question 11.
meta.format_note: Needs drawn solution: bearings problem, a labelled diagram (north lines, $29^\circ$, $31^\circ$, $60^\circ$, sides $12$ and $20$) should sit at the top (key 382_q19_s1).

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$ with $\angle ABC=60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 12^2+20^2-2\times 12\times 20\cos 60^\circ \\ &= 304 \\ AC &= \sqrt{304} \\ &= 4\sqrt{19} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{total distance} &= 12+20+4\sqrt{19} \\ &= 32+4\sqrt{19}\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
This is $49.4355937\ldots\approx 49.44$ km.
criteria: Uses the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

1767.stem:
A random variable is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The table gives the probability that this random variable is less than $z$ for different values of $z$.

\extable{382_q20_t1}

In a particular city, the weekly rents for apartments are normally distributed with a mean of \$750 and a standard deviation of \$100.

parts.latex: Find the probability that the weekly rent of an apartment chosen at random is less than \$600.

Sam’s budget for the weekly rent is \$600. She has refined her searches and produced a list such that she is only looking at properties which are less than the mean weekly rent. Find the probability that an apartment that Sam chooses at random from this list is within her budget.

solutions.latex:
Standardise using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}=\dfrac{600-750}{100}=-1.5$, then use the symmetry of the normal curve, $P(Z<-1.5)=1-P(Z<1.5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<600) &= P(Z<-1.5) \\ &= 1-P(Z<1.5) \\ &= 1-0.933 \\ &= 0.067 \\ &= 6.7\% \end{aligned}$$

The mean is $750$, so by symmetry $P(X<750)=0.5$. Using conditional probability, $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<600\mid X<750) &= \dfrac{P(X<600\cap X<750)}{P(X<750)} \\ &= \dfrac{P(X<600)}{P(X<750)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.067}{0.5} \\ &= 0.134 \\ &= 13.4\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct conditional probability set-up, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: regular octahedron ABCDE with centre O, edge 6 cm, M midpoint of BC, dashed AM and ME

parts.latex:
Two identical right pyramids with square bases and equilateral triangular faces are joined to form a regular octahedron.

The following diagram shows a regular octahedron with edge length 6 cm and centre at $O$. $AM$ and $ME$ are perpendicular heights of $\Delta ABC$ and $\Delta BCE$ respectively and point $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

\exfigure{382_q21_1}

Find the size of $\angle AME$, to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
By symmetry $\triangle AMO\cong\triangle EMO$ (SSS: $AM=EM$, $AO=EO$, $MO$ common), so
$$\angle AME=2\times\angle AMO$$
In $\triangle AMC$ ($\angle AMC=90^\circ$, $AC=6$, $MC=3$), by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} AM &= \sqrt{6^2-3^2} \\ &= \sqrt{27} \\ &= 3\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle AMO$ (right angle at $O$, with $MO=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6=3$, half the side of the square base):
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle AMO &= \dfrac{MO}{AM} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \angle AMO &= \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle AME &= 2\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\ &= 109.4712\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 109^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Accept an alternative using the sine rule (finding $AM$ and $AE$, then the angle).

1769.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{kx}{x^2+1}, & \text{for } 1\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 13}$.
Find the median $m$.

solutions.latex:
Since $f(x)$ is a probability density function, the total area under it is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5\dfrac{kx}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^5\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 1 &&(\text{the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, up to the factor }2) \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln\left(x^2+1\right)\Big]_1^5 &= 1 \\ k(\ln 26-\ln 2) &= 2 \\ k\ln 13 &= 2 &&(\text{log law}: \ln 26-\ln 2=\ln 13) \\ k &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 13} \end{aligned}$$

The median $m$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_1^m f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}$, using $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 13}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{\ln 13}\int_1^m\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 0.5 \\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 13}\Big[\ln\left(x^2+1\right)\Big]_1^m &= 0.5 \\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 13}\left(\ln\left(m^2+1\right)-\ln 2\right) &= 0.5 \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{m^2+1}{2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 13 \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{m^2+1}{2}\right) &= \ln 13^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ \dfrac{m^2+1}{2} &= \sqrt{13} \\ m^2+1 &= 2\sqrt{13} \\ m^2 &= 2\sqrt{13}-1 \\ m &= \sqrt{2\sqrt{13}-1} &&(1\le m\le 5,\text{ so the positive root}) \end{aligned}$$
So $m=2.492208\ldots$

1770.stem: The motion of a particle is given by $x=10t+4e^{-3.5t}-4$, where $x$ is the displacement from the starting position in metres and $t$ is time after the initial position in seconds.

figures.cap: solution sketch: dx/dt against t: y-intercept -4, asymptote dx/dt = 10, t-intercept -(2/7) ln(5/7)

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.
Sketch the velocity-time graph.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-3.5t}\right)=-3.5e^{-3.5t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10+4\times(-3.5)e^{-3.5t} \\ &= 10-14e^{-3.5t} \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10-14e^0 \\ &= -4\text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), the velocity is $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=10-14e^{-3.5t}$.

As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-3.5t}\to 0$, so $v\to 10$: the graph has the horizontal asymptote $v=10$.

The $t$-intercept is where $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10-14e^{-3.5t} &= 0 \\ e^{-3.5t} &= \dfrac{5}{7} \\ -3.5t &= \ln\dfrac{5}{7} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{5}{7}}{-3.5} \\ &= -\dfrac{2\ln\frac{5}{7}}{7} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{382_q23_s1}

meta.corrected: Source line ‘dx/dt = 10 + 4x - 3.5e^{-3.5t}’ is a slip for 10 + 4(-3.5)e^{-3.5t}; written as the correct derivative.

parts.latex: Let $f(x)$ be an even function. If $\displaystyle\int_0^6 f(x)\,dx=12$ and $\displaystyle\int_4^6 f(x)\,dx=-5$ evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4} 2f(x)\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Split the integral from $0$ to $6$ at $4$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx &= \int_0^6 f(x)\,dx-\int_4^6 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 12-(-5) \\ &= 17 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-4}^{4}2f(x)\,dx &= 2\int_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times 2\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times 2\times 17 \\ &= 68 \end{aligned}$$

1772.stem:
At a market, a stallholder is hosting free-to-play mini games.

If the player wins against the stallholder, they will receive \$25 as a reward. If they lose, they have to pay \$5 to the stallholder. If the game ends in a draw, no money is exchanged.

The random variable $X$ represents the amount of money a player wins per mini game, where the probability of winning a game is independent of each other.

The distribution of $X$ is given in the table below.

\extable{382_q25_t1}

parts.latex: Show that $2k^2-k+0.12=0$.
Find the value of $k$, giving reasons for your answer.
Find $E(X)$.

A player decides to play 3 mini games.

How much is the player expected to win or lose?
What is the probability that the player will lose exactly two of the three games?

solutions.latex:
The probabilities in the distribution add to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sum P(X=x) &= 1 \\ \left(0.29-2k^2\right)+0.87+(k-0.28) &= 1 \\ 0.88-2k^2+k &= 1 \\ \therefore\ 2k^2-k+0.12 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Using the quadratic formula on $2k^2-k+0.12=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{1-4\times 2\times 0.12}}{2\times 2} \\ &= \dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{0.04}}{4} \\ &= 0.3\text{ or }0.2 \end{aligned}$$
$P(X=25)=k-0.28$ must satisfy $0\le k-0.28\le 1$, so $0.28\le k\le 1.28$. This rules out $k=0.2$ (it gives a negative probability).
$$\therefore\ k=0.3$$

Expected values add over games, so for $3$ games the expected amount is $3E(X)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3E(X) &= 3\times(-0.05) \\ &= -\$0.15 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the player is expected to lose $15$ cents.

A player loses a game when $X=-5$, with probability $P(\text{L})=0.29-2(0.3)^2=0.11$. The games are independent, and exactly two losses can happen in three ways: $\text{LL}\overline{\text{L}}$, $\text{L}\overline{\text{L}}\text{L}$, $\overline{\text{L}}\text{LL}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{lose exactly twice}) &= 3\times(0.11)^2\times(1-0.11) \\ &= 0.032307 \\ &= 3.2307\% \end{aligned}$$

1773.stem:
A spring is extended to its maximum length and released.

The length of the spring $l$ cm, $t$ seconds after release is modelled by the function $l=a+b\cos 2t$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: l = 7 + 4 cos 2t on 0 to 2 pi, maximum 11, minimum 3, centre line 7

parts.latex: Given that the minimum length of the spring is 3 cm and the maximum length is 11 cm, find the values of $a$ and $b$.
Sketch a graph of the model in the domain $0\le t\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
The centre line is halfway between the maximum and minimum lengths, and the amplitude is half their difference. The spring starts at its maximum length, so $b>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{11+3}{2} \\ &= 7 \\ b &= \dfrac{11-3}{2} \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $l=7+4\cos 2t$. Its period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$, so the domain $0\le t\le 2\pi$ covers two full cycles.

\exfigure{382_q26_s1}

parts.latex: List a set of transformations that, when applied in order, would transform $f(x)$ to $f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}-1\right)$.
Find the equation of $y=f(x)$.

solutions.latex:
Method 1:

First translate right by $1$ unit, giving $f(x-1)$.

Then dilate horizontally by a factor of $3$ (replace $x$ with $\dfrac{x}{3}$), giving $f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}-1\right)$.

Method 2: write $f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}-1\right)=f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}(x-3)\right)$.

First dilate horizontally by a factor of $3$, giving $f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)$.

Then translate right by $3$ units (replace $x$ with $x-3$), giving $f\left(\dfrac{x-3}{3}\right)=f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}-1\right)$.
criteria: One correct transformation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Method 1: undo the transformations in reverse order. A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ replaces $x$ with $3x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}-1\right) &= \dfrac{1}{x-2}-6 \\ f(x-1) &= f\left(\dfrac{3x}{3}-1\right) &&(\text{dilate horizontally by a factor of }\dfrac{1}{3}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3x-2}-6 \end{aligned}$$
Translating left by $1$ unit replaces $x$ with $x+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= f\big((x+1)-1\big) &&(\text{translate left by }1\text{ unit}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3(x+1)-2}-6 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3x+1}-6 \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: undo in the other order. Translating left by $3$ units replaces $x$ with $x+3$:
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= f\left(\dfrac{x+3}{3}-1\right) &&(\text{translate left by }3\text{ units}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x-2+3}-6 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x+1}-6 \end{aligned}$$
Then a horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ replaces $x$ with $3x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= f\left(\dfrac{3x}{3}\right) &&(\text{dilate horizontally by a factor of }\dfrac{1}{3}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3x+1}-6 \end{aligned}$$
Both methods give $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3x+1}-6$.
criteria: Correct first step, or equivalent merit

meta.verify_fix: Method 2 last step read f(3x/3-1) (that is f(x-1)); now f(3x/3)

figures.cap: quadrant of radius 3 with an inscribed rectangle of length x and width y

parts.latex:
Show that the area of the rectangle is given by

$$A=x\sqrt{9-x^2}$$

Show that

$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\sqrt{9-x^2}-\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}$$
Hence find the maximum area of the rectangle.

solutions.latex:
Since $x^2+y^2=9$:
$$\begin{aligned} y^2 &= 9-x^2 \\ y &= \sqrt{9-x^2} &&(y\text{ is a length, so positive}) \end{aligned}$$
The area of the rectangle is length times width:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= xy \\ &= x\sqrt{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=(9-x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}(9-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot(-2x)=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ is found by the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= u'v+uv' \\ &= 1\cdot\sqrt{9-x^2}+x\cdot\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}} \\ &= \sqrt{9-x^2}-\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$

For a maximum or minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$ (using part (b)):
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{9-x^2}-\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}} &= 0 \\ 9-x^2-x^2 &= 0 &&(\text{multiply by }\sqrt{9-x^2}) \\ 9-2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{9}{2} \\ x &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} &&(x\text{ is a length, so positive}) \\ &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature of the stationary point with the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side of $x=\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$:

\extable{Ts2638_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $A$ is a maximum when $x=\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\max} &= x\sqrt{9-x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{9-\dfrac{9}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{9}{2}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $x=\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ and tests the nature, or equivalent merit
Sets $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$ and simplifies, or equivalent merit

1776.stem: The first three terms of a geometric series are $6\cos\theta$, $2(\sin\theta-2)$ and $3\tan\theta$.

parts.latex: Show that $2\sin^2\theta-17\sin\theta+8=0$.
Find the exact value of $\theta$ in radians, given that it is obtuse.
Find the limiting sum of the series, leaving your answer in the form $k\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right)$.

solutions.latex:
In a geometric series the ratio of consecutive terms is constant, so $\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3\tan\theta}{2(\sin\theta-2)} &= \dfrac{2(\sin\theta-2)}{6\cos\theta} \\ 18\tan\theta\cos\theta &= 4(\sin\theta-2)^2 \\ 9\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cos\theta &= 2\left(\sin^2\theta-4\sin\theta+4\right) &&\left(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) \\ 9\sin\theta &= 2\sin^2\theta-8\sin\theta+8 \\ 2\sin^2\theta-17\sin\theta+8 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct ratio equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\theta$ is obtuse, $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\pi$. Let $m=\sin\theta$ in the equation from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} 2m^2-17m+8 &= 0 \\ (2m-1)(m-8) &= 0 \\ m &= \dfrac{1}{2}\text{ or }m=8 \end{aligned}$$
$\sin\theta=8$ has no solution, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The obtuse angle with this sine is
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &= \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

The first term is $a=T_1=6\cos\theta$ with $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, and the ratio is $r=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 6\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ &= 6\times\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= -3\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{2\left(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}-2\right)}{-3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\left(\frac{1}{2}-2\right)}{-3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{-3}{-3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists, $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{-3\sqrt{3}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{-9}{\sqrt{3}-1}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}+1} \\ &= \dfrac{-9\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right)}{2} \\ &= -\dfrac{9}{2}\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right) \end{aligned}$$

1777.stem:
The shaded region is enclosed by the curve $y=3\ln x$ and line $y=(x-1)\ln 4$, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{382_q30_1}

figures.cap: curve y = 3 ln x and line y = (x-1) ln 4 meeting at x = 1 and x = 4, region between them shaded
solution sketch: y = 3 ln x - (x-1) ln 4 from 1 to 4 with trapezium chords at 2 and 3

parts.latex: Use the Trapezoidal rule with 3 sub-intervals to find an approximate area of the shaded region. Give your answer correct to three significant figures.
Explain whether the approximation is an overestimate or underestimate of the true area of the shaded region.

solutions.latex:
The curve and the line meet at $x=1$ and $x=4$, so the shaded area is
$$A=\int_1^4\Big(3\ln x-(x-1)\ln 4\Big)\,dx$$
With $3$ sub-intervals the width is $h=\dfrac{4-1}{3}=1$, so the function values of $y=3\ln x-(x-1)\ln 4$ at $x=1,2,3,4$ are:

\extable{Ts2642_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{4-1}{2\times 3}\Big[0+0+2\big(3\ln 2-\ln 4+3\ln 3-2\ln 4\big)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\Big(2\big(3\ln 2-3\ln 4+3\ln 3\big)\Big) \\ &= 1.216395\ldots \\ &\approx 1.22\text{ units}^2\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area under $y=\ln x$, then subtract the area of the triangle.
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
Sets up the area integral or the table of values, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: Source 'Method 2' says to estimate the area under $y=\ln x$ and subtract the triangle. The curve in the question is $y=3\ln x$, so that probably means $y=3\ln x$ (with the triangle under the line $y=(x-1)\ln 4$). Kept as written. Method 1 checks numerically: $3\ln\dfrac{3}{2}=1.2164$.

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x)=3\ln x$ and $g(x)=(x-1)\ln 4$. For $1\le x\le 4$, $f(x)$ is concave down ($f''(x)=-\dfrac{3}{x^2}<0$) and $g(x)$ is a straight line, so it has zero concavity.

Hence $f(x)-g(x)$ is concave down for $1\le x\le 4$, so the chords of the trapezoidal rule lie below the curve. The approximation of
$$\int_1^4\big(f(x)-g(x)\big)\,dx$$
is an underestimate.

Alternatively, the graph of $y=f(x)-g(x)=3\ln x-(x-1)\ln 4$ is concave down:

\exfigure{382_q30_s1}

Another way: $y=3\ln x$ is concave down, so the trapezoidal rule underestimates the area under it. The area of the triangle under the line is exact, so the approximation of the shaded area is also an underestimate.

meta.marker_note: Half a mark for stating that $f$ is concave down and $g$ has zero concavity.

1778.stem: Let $A$ and $B$ be two events. Suppose that $P(A)=0.8$, $P(B\mid A)=0.45$ and $P(B\mid\overline{A})=0.6$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram of A and B with P(A and B) = 0.36 and P(not A and B) = 0.12

parts.latex: Find $P(B)$.
Is event $A$ independent from event $B$? Justify your answer with relevant calculations.

solutions.latex:
Use $P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}$ and the same formula for $\overline{A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B\mid A) &= \dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)} \\ 0.45 &= \dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{0.8} \\ P(B\cap A) &= 0.36 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(B\mid\overline{A}) &= \dfrac{P(B\cap\overline{A})}{P(\overline{A})} \\ 0.6 &= \dfrac{P(B\cap\overline{A})}{1-0.8} \\ P(B\cap\overline{A}) &= 0.12 \end{aligned}$$
$B$ happens either with $A$ or with $\overline{A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B) &= P(A\cap B)+P(\overline{A}\cap B) \\ &= 0.36+0.12 \\ &= 0.48 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{382_q31_s1}
criteria: Finds one of them, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Needs drawn solution: \exfigure{382_q31_s1} is kept (the source's own diagram for this part, presumably the tree) but has no redraw yet (no .tex in state/tikz/tex).

solutions.latex:
Events $A$ and $B$ are independent only if $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Here
$$\begin{aligned} P(A)\times P(B) &= 0.8\times 0.48 \\ &= 0.384 \\ &\ne 0.36=P(A\cap B) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $A$ is NOT independent of $B$.

figures.cap: graph of y = x e^(mx) with the region between the curve, the x-axis and x = 1 shaded

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{mx}\right)$.
Hence find $\displaystyle\int xe^{mx}\,dx$.

The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=xe^{mx}$, the $x$-axis and $x=1$ is shown below. Given that the area of this area is $\dfrac{1}{m}$, find $m$.

\exfigure{382_q32_1}

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{mx}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=me^{mx}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{mx}\right) &= 1\cdot e^{mx}+x\cdot me^{mx} \\ &= e^{mx}+mxe^{mx} \end{aligned}$$

Integrate both sides of the result of part (a) with respect to $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} xe^{mx} &= \int\left(e^{mx}+mxe^{mx}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{m}e^{mx}+m\int xe^{mx}\,dx \end{aligned}$$
Make the integral the subject (the constant of integration is added at the end):
$$\begin{aligned} m\int xe^{mx}\,dx &= xe^{mx}-\dfrac{1}{m}e^{mx} \\ \int xe^{mx}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{m}e^{mx}\left(x-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates both sides, or work of equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve passes through the origin, so the region runs from $x=0$ to $x=1$. Using part (b), with area $\dfrac{1}{m}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^1 xe^{mx}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{m} \\ \dfrac{1}{m}\left[e^{mx}\left(x-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)\right]_0^1 &= \dfrac{1}{m} \\ e^m\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)-e^0\left(0-\dfrac{1}{m}\right) &= 1 &&(\text{multiply by }m) \\ e^m\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)+\dfrac{1}{m}-1 &= 0 \\ e^m\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)-\left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right) &= 0 \\ \left(1-\dfrac{1}{m}\right)\left(e^m-1\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $1-\dfrac{1}{m}=0$ or $e^m=1$, giving $m=1$ or $m=0$. But $m\ne 0$, since the area is $\dfrac{1}{m}$.
$$\therefore\ m=1$$

382_q32_1.notes: y = xe^{mx} drawn with m = 1 (the crop's minimum sits at x = -1, and m = 1 is also the answer), axis scales taken from the crop (x 112 px/unit, y 63.7 px/unit); region 0..1 shaded house grey; x = 1 dashed (aux) with both arrows as on paper; dot at (1,0). Curve 0.9pt. Rules 1,3,4,5,9,10,16,19.

parts.latex: What is the domain of $f(x)=\sqrt{4x-8}$?

solutions.latex:
The square root $\sqrt{4x-8}$ needs $4x-8\ge 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x-8 &\ge 0 \\ 4x &\ge 8 &&(\text{add }8) \\ x &\ge 2 &&(\text{divide by }4) \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graph of an exponential curve with horizontal asymptote y=-2 passing through (-1,0)

solutions.latex:
The graph has the horizontal asymptote $y=-2$, and $y=2e^{x+b}+c$ has the asymptote $y=c$, so $c=-2$ and $y=2e^{x+b}-2$.

The curve passes through $(-1,0)$:

parts.latex:
Consider the sequence,

$$\log_2 3,\ \log_2 9,\ \log_2 27\ \ldots$$

What is the sum of the first 10 terms of this sequence?

solutions.latex:
By the log power law, $\log_2 9=2\log_2 3$ and $\log_2 27=3\log_2 3$, so the terms are
$$\log_2 3,\ 2\log_2 3,\ 3\log_2 3,\ \ldots$$
This is an arithmetic sequence with $a=\log_2 3$ and $d=\log_2 3$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}\big[2a+9d\big] \\ &= 5\big[2\log_2 3+9\log_2 3\big] \\ &= 55\log_2 3 \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graphs of y=|x| and y=2-x^2

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $|x|=2-x^2$. For $x\ge 0$ this is $x=2-x^2$, so $x^2+x-2=0$, $(x+2)(x-1)=0$, giving $x=1$. By symmetry the other intersection is $x=-1$.

Between the intersections the parabola is above $y=|x|$, and the region is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\int_0^1 \big((2-x^2)-x\big)\,dx \\ &= 2\left[2x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1 \\ &= 2\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7}{3}\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the area is $\dfrac{7}{3}$ units$^2$.

meta.self_check: Integral evaluated by hand and in python (2.3333 = 7/3); agrees with key C.

parts.latex:
For two functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$, it is known that for all $a>0$, $g(a)>h(a)$.

It is also known that $h'(x)<0$ and $g'(x)>0$ for $x>0$.

How many solutions are there to $g(x)-h(x)=0$ in the domain $a>0$?

solutions.latex:
Let $d(x)=g(x)-h(x)$. Then $d'(x)=g'(x)-h'(x)$.

For $x>0$, $g'(x)>0$ and $h'(x)<0$, so $d'(x)>0$.

Also $g(a)>h(a)$ for all $a>0$, so $d(x)>0$ for every $x>0$.

Hence $g(x)-h(x)=0$ has no solution in $x>0$ (the difference never reaches $0$).

meta.self_check: Logical argument: d>0 on the whole domain, so no zero. Agrees with key A (monotonicity is not even needed).

parts.latex: Which of the following shows the graph of $f(x)=2^x$ and its derivative on the same plane?

solutions.latex:
For $f(x)=2^x$, $f'(x)=2^x\ln 2$.

At $x=0$: $f(0)=1$ and $f'(0)=\ln 2\approx 0.69$, so the derivative has the smaller $y$-intercept.

Since $\ln 2<1$, $f'(x)=(\ln 2)f(x)<f(x)$ for all $x$: the derivative curve lies below $f(x)$ everywhere and never crosses it.

Both curves are positive and increasing. Only graph A shows $f'(x)$ below $f(x)$ with no intersection.

The other graphs have $f'$ above $f$ (B) or the two curves crossing at $x=0$ (C and D), which would need $f'(0)=f(0)$.

parts.latex: If $f(x)=x(x-1)$ how many different solutions are there to the equation $f(x^2)=0$?

Replace $x$ with $x^2$ in $f(x)=x(x-1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(x^2\right) &= x^2\left(x^2-1\right) = 0 \\ x^2 &= 0\text{ or }1 \\ x &= 0,\ \pm 1 \end{aligned}$$
So there are three different solutions.

parts.latex: Find the equation relating $x$ and $y$.
Graph the relationship showing two different points on the graph.

solutions.latex:
$y$ is inversely proportional to $x$, so $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$, that is $xy=k$. Substitute $x=8$, $y=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} xy &= k \\ k &= 8\times 2 \\ &= 16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{16}{x}$$

parts.latex: Complete a possible sequence of transformations that maps $f(x)$ to $g(x)$.

On the same set of axes below, sketch the graph of $y=g(x)$ below.

\exfigure{369_q13_1}

solutions.latex:
Write $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}f(2-x)=\dfrac{1}{2}f\big(-(x-2)\big)$.

Reflect $f(x)$ in the $y$-axis, giving $f(-x)$.

Translate $2$ units to the right, giving $f\big(-(x-2)\big)=f(2-x)$.

Vertically dilate by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, giving $g(x)$.

Alternatively, $f(2-x)=(-1-x)^2-1=(x+1)^2-1=f(x+4)$, since $f$ is symmetric about $x=3$.

Translate $4$ units to the left, giving $f(x+4)$.

Vertically dilate by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, giving $g(x)$.

meta.marker_note: Some solutions had the incorrect direction, or dilation factor, which cost one mark. Only correct answers from the given equation in the question received marks.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}f(x+4)$:
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[(x+4-3)^2-1\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(x+1)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
In turning-point form, the vertex is $\left(-1,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

$x$-intercepts: $g(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}(x+1)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}&=0\\ (x+1)^2&=1\\ x+1&=\pm1\\ x&=-2\ \text{ or }\ x=0\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{369_q13_s1}

parts.latex: Solve $\log_2(x+3)-\log_2 x=1$

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms need $x+3>0$ and $x>0$, so $x>0$. Using the log law $\log_a m-\log_a n=\log_a\dfrac{m}{n}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_2(x+3)-\log_2 x &= 1 \\ \log_2\dfrac{x+3}{x} &= 1 \\ \dfrac{x+3}{x} &= 2^1 \\ x+3 &= 2x \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
This satisfies $x>0$.

parts.latex: An investment of \$4000 earns interest at a rate of $r\%$ p.a. over a period of one year. How much more interest would the investment earn, if interest is compounded half-yearly rather than yearly? Find the answer in terms of $r$.

solutions.latex:
With yearly compounding at $\dfrac{r}{100}$:
$$A_1=4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}\right)$$
With half-yearly compounding the rate per half-year is $\dfrac{r}{200}$, for $2$ periods:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= 4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{200}\right)^2 \\ &= 4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}+\dfrac{r^2}{40000}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The extra interest is
$$\begin{aligned} A_2-A_1 &= 4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}+\dfrac{r^2}{40000}\right)-4000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}\right) \\ &= 4000\cdot\dfrac{r^2}{40000} \\ &= \dfrac{r^2}{10} \end{aligned}$$
So the investment earns $\$\dfrac{r^2}{10}$ more.

meta.top_criterion_original: Marker comments: Many students recognised that the interest rate is halved for the half yearly case. The better solutions considered $r$ as a percentage, $\dfrac{r}{100}$ in the calculations. Some solutions considered $n$ number of terms, which did not get to any results.

parts.latex: Solve $2\sin^2 x-1=0$ for $-180^\circ\le x\le180^\circ$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin^2 x-1 &= 0 \\ \sin^2 x &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \sin x &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $45^\circ$, and $\sin x$ takes both signs, so there is a solution in each quadrant:
$$x=\pm 45^\circ,\ \pm 135^\circ$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=(2-x)^4$ at the point $(3,1)$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$y'=4(2-x)^3\cdot(-1)=-4(2-x)^3$$
At $x=3$ the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} m &= -4(2-3)^3 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Using the point $(3,1)$:

parts.latex: Given $\tan\alpha=-0.2$ and $\sin\alpha>0$, find the exact value of $\cos\alpha$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan\alpha<0$ and $\sin\alpha>0$, the angle $\alpha$ is in the second quadrant, where $\cos\alpha$ is negative.

$\tan\alpha=-0.2=-\dfrac{1}{5}$, so in the related right-angled triangle the opposite side is $1$ and the adjacent side is $5$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\text{hypotenuse}=\sqrt{1^2+5^2}=\sqrt{26}$$
$$\therefore\ \cos\alpha=-\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{26}}$$
criteria: Correct working for finding the value

parts.latex: Find the global maximum of the function $y=x^2(x+2)^3$ for $-3\le x\le1$.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{369_q20_s1}

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=(x+2)^3\\ u'&=2x & v'&=3(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2x(x+2)^3+3(x+2)^2x^2 \\ &= x(x+2)^2\big(2(x+2)+3x\big) \\ &= x(x+2)^2(5x+4) \end{aligned}$$
$y'=0$ when $x=0$, $x=-2$ or $x=-0.8$. Since $(x+2)^2\ge 0$, the sign of $y'$ is the sign of $x(5x+4)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &> 0 &&\text{for } x<-2\text{ and }-2<x<-0.8 \\ y' &< 0 &&\text{for } -0.8<x<0 \\ y' &> 0 &&\text{for } x>0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-2$ is a horizontal point of inflexion ($y'$ does not change sign), $x=0$ is a minimum turning point and $x=-0.8$ is a maximum turning point.

The global maximum is at a maximum turning point or an endpoint, so test $x=-0.8$ and the endpoints:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-0.8:&\quad y=1.10592 \\ x=-3:&\quad y=-9 \\ x=1:&\quad y=27 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the global maximum is }27$$
criteria: Correct working, however did not state the global maximum or did not use the correct reasoning for turning points, or equivalent
Correct working, however only uses the stationary points to state the global maximum, or equivalent. Did not test the endpoints and did not state the global maximum
Correct derivative or tests endpoints, but makes no further progress

parts.latex: Differentiate $\sqrt{3+x^3}$.
Hence, find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{3+x^3}}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Write $y=(3+x^3)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and use the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{1}{2}(3+x^3)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot 3x^2 \\ &= \dfrac{3x^2}{2\sqrt{3+x^3}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the chain rule, however did not simplify

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source simplified to $\dfrac{3}{2\left(\sqrt{3}+x^3\right)}$, which is wrong (the $x^2$ is lost and the root covers only the $3$). Now $\dfrac{3x^2}{2\sqrt{3+x^3}}$, which is the form part (b) needs.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{3+x^3}=\dfrac{3x^2}{2\sqrt{3+x^3}}$. Multiply and divide the integrand by constants to match this:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{3+x^3}}\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{3}\int\dfrac{3x^2}{2\sqrt{3+x^3}}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{3+x^3}+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Multiplies the integral by $\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $\dfrac{2}{3}$, or equivalent

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3\dfrac{24x^2-14}{4x^3-7x+5}\,dx$ leaving your answer in simplest exact form.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of the denominator is $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(4x^3-7x+5\right)=12x^2-7$, and the numerator is twice this, so use $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3\dfrac{24x^2-14}{4x^3-7x+5}\,dx &= 2\int_1^3\dfrac{12x^2-7}{4x^3-7x+5}\,dx \\ &= 2\Big[\ln\left|4x^3-7x+5\right|\Big]_1^3 \\ &= 2\big(\ln 92-\ln 2\big) \\ &= 2\ln 46 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Factors out a $2$ from the numerator

parts.latex: Show that $\cos\theta=\dfrac{3x-10}{2x}$.
If the area of the triangle is $A$, show that $A^2=-20(x^2-12x+20)$.
Find the values of $x$ and $y$ when the area is a maximum.

solutions.latex:
Use the cosine rule in $\triangle XYZ$, with $\theta$ between the sides $8$ and $x$ and opposite the side $y$. The perimeter is $20$, so $8+x+y=20$ and $y=12-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta &= \dfrac{8^2+x^2-y^2}{2\times 8\times x} \\ &= \dfrac{64+x^2-(12-x)^2}{16x} \\ &= \dfrac{64+x^2-144+24x-x^2}{16x} \\ &= \dfrac{24x-80}{16x} \\ &= \dfrac{3x-10}{2x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule and substitution of $y=12-x$, however no further progress is made

solutions.latex:
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with the sides $8$ and $x$ enclosing $\theta$, then $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 8\times x\sin\theta \\ &= 4x\sin\theta \\ A^2 &= 16x^2\sin^2\theta \\ &= 16x^2\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right) \\ &= 16x^2\left[1-\dfrac{(3x-10)^2}{4x^2}\right] \\ &= 16x^2-4(3x-10)^2 \\ &= 16x^2-4\left(9x^2-60x+100\right) \\ &= 16x^2-36x^2+240x-400 \\ &= -20x^2+240x-400 \\ &= -20\left(x^2-12x+20\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the area formula and substitution of $\cos^2\theta$, but does not progress to the required solution

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source working had errors between its first and last lines ($A^2=16x^2-16\cos^2\theta$ lost the $x^2$ factor; then $-4x^2\left(9x^2-60x+100\right)$ should be $-4(3x-10)^2$ expanded as $-4\left(9x^2-60x+100\right)$; and $+400$ should be $-400$, since $-20\left(x^2-12x+20\right)=-20x^2+240x-400$). The first and last lines were right; the steps between are now correct.

solutions.latex:
$A>0$, so $A$ is greatest when $A^2$ is greatest. From part (b), let $A^2=f(x)=-20x^2+240x-400$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -40x+240 \\ f'(x) &= 0\text{ when }x=6 \\ f''(x) &= -40<0 \end{aligned}$$
So a maximum occurs at $x=6$. The perimeter gives $y=12-x$, so when $x=6$, $y=6$.

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A}{\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A}\equiv\sec^2A$.
Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int\tan^2x\left(\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Write cosec and $\sin$ in terms of $\sin A$, then multiply the top and bottom by $\sin A$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A}{\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{\sin A}}{\frac{1}{\sin A}-\sin A} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2 A} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A} &&(\sin^2 A+\cos^2 A=1) \\ &= \sec^2 A \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the LHS in terms of $\sin A$

solutions.latex:
By part (a), $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}=\sec^2 x$. Using $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx=\dfrac{1}{n+1}[f(x)]^{n+1}+c$ for $n\ne -1$ (reference sheet), with $f(x)=\tan x$ and $f'(x)=\sec^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\tan^2 x\,\sec^2 x\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{3}\tan^3 x+C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Let $\log_b x=\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $\log_b y=\dfrac{1}{4}$. Find the value of $\log_b\left(\dfrac{b^3\sqrt{x}}{y}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log_b(xy)=\log_b x+\log_b y$, $\log_b\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)=\log_b x-\log_b y$ and $\log_b x^n=n\log_b x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_b\left(\dfrac{b^3\sqrt{x}}{y}\right) &= \log_b b^3+\dfrac{1}{2}\log_b x-\log_b y \\ &= 3+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &= 3+\dfrac{1}{6}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{35}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the log laws and substitutes, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The diagram shows a shape that consists of a square with two identical arcs on opposite sides of the square.

\exfigure{369_q27_1}

The square has a side length of 12m and the arcs have their centre at the centre of the square.

The points E, F, G and H are the endpoints of the arcs.

AE = FB = CG = HD = 1 m.

Calculate the area of the shape, to the nearest m$^2$.

solutions.latex:
The shape is the square plus two identical circular segments, one on each of the sides $AD$ and $BC$.

Take the centre $O$ of the square as origin. $E$ is $6$ m horizontally and $5$ m vertically from $O$ (the half-side is $6$ and $AE=1$), so by Pythagoras the radius is
$$r=OE=\sqrt{6^2+5^2}=\sqrt{61}$$
Let $\angle EOH=2\theta$. In the right-angled triangle formed by half of chord $EH$ (length $5$):
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{6},\quad \theta\approx 0.6947,\quad 2\theta\approx 1.3895\text{ rad}$$
Area of one segment, using $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\phi-\sin\phi)$ with $\phi=2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{seg}} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(61)\left(1.3895-\sin 1.3895\right) \\ &\approx 30.5\times 0.4059 \\ &\approx 12.38\text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Total area:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 12^2+2(12.38) \\ &\approx 168.76 \\ &\approx 169\text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of one segment, or equivalent merit
Finds the radius $\sqrt{61}$ or the angle $\angle EOH$, or equivalent merit

1807.stem:
Preeti deposits \$300 into a savings account on 1 January 2024. The account accrues interest at the rate of $3.6\%$ p.a. compounding monthly. Preeti plans to deposit \$300 at the start of every month thereafter until the end of 2029.

Let $A_n$ be the amount that Preeti has in her account at the end of the $n$th month (where the 1$^{\text{st}}$ month is January 2024).

parts.latex: By first obtaining expressions for $A_1$, $A_2$, and $A_3$, show that $A_n=100300(1.003^n-1)$

Preeti quits her job and goes to university for two years starting in 2028. As a result, she is unable to make any monthly deposits in the years 2028-2029. However, while she is at university, her bank offers her a special interest rate of $6\%$ p.a. compounding monthly.

Calculate the value of Preeti’s account at the end of 2029, and find how much more money she would have had if she hadn’t gone to university.

solutions.latex:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{3.6\%}{12}=0.3\%=0.003$, so each month's balance is multiplied by $1.003$.

Each deposit of \$300 is made at the start of the month, so it earns interest for that month.
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 300(1.003) \\ A_2 &= \big(A_1+300\big)(1.003) \\ &= 300(1.003^2+1.003) \\ A_3 &= \big(A_2+300\big)(1.003) \\ &= 300(1.003^3+1.003^2+1.003) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$A_n=300\left(1.003^n+1.003^{n-1}+\cdots+1.003\right)$$
This is a geometric series with first term $a=300(1.003)$, common ratio $r=1.003$ and $n$ terms.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= \dfrac{300(1.003)\left(1.003^n-1\right)}{1.003-1} \\ &= \dfrac{300.9}{0.003}\left(1.003^n-1\right) \\ &= 100300\left(1.003^n-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Obtains the expression for $A_n$ as a geometric series, or equivalent merit
Obtains correct expressions for $A_1$, $A_2$ and $A_3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Deposits are made for $2024$ to $2027$, which is $4\times 12=48$ months. The balance at the end of $2027$ is
$$\begin{aligned} A_{48} &= 100300\left(1.003^{48}-1\right) \\ &\approx \$15\,509.91 \end{aligned}$$
For $2028$ and $2029$ there are no deposits, $24$ months at $\dfrac{6\%}{12}=0.5\%$ per month:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Value at end of 2029} &= 15\,509.91\times 1.005^{24} \\ &\approx \$17\,482.14 \end{aligned}$$
If she had not gone to university, deposits continue for $72$ months at $0.3\%$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{72} &= 100300\left(1.003^{72}-1\right) \\ &\approx \$24\,142.32 \end{aligned}$$
Difference:
$$24\,142.32-17\,482.14\approx \$6660.18$$
Hence her account is worth about $\$17\,482.14$, and she would have had about $\$6660.18$ more.
criteria: Finds the value at the end of $2029$ and attempts $A_{72}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A random variable is defined by the probability distribution:

$$P(X=x)=\dfrac{x^2+x}{20}\ \text{ for } x=1,2,3.$$

Find the value of $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

solutions.latex:
Find each probability:
$$P(X=1)=\dfrac{2}{20},\quad P(X=2)=\dfrac{6}{20},\quad P(X=3)=\dfrac{12}{20}$$
These sum to $1$, so the distribution is valid. Using $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1\left(\dfrac{2}{20}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{6}{20}\right)+3\left(\dfrac{12}{20}\right)=\dfrac{50}{20}=2.5 \\ E(X^2) &= 1\left(\dfrac{2}{20}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{6}{20}\right)+9\left(\dfrac{12}{20}\right)=\dfrac{134}{20}=6.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) &= 6.7-2.5^2 \\ &= 0.45 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the probabilities or $E(X)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Two events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A)=p$, $P(B)=2p-\dfrac{5}{6}$ and $P\left(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\right)=p^2-\dfrac{5}{18}$.

Find the value of $p$.

solutions.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are independent, so $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{B}$ are independent:
$$P\left(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\right)=P\left(\overline{A}\right)\times P\left(\overline{B}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} p^2-\dfrac{5}{18} &= (1-p)\left(1-2p+\dfrac{5}{6}\right) \\ p^2-\dfrac{5}{18} &= (1-p)\left(\dfrac{11}{6}-2p\right) \\ p^2-\dfrac{5}{18} &= \dfrac{11}{6}-\dfrac{23p}{6}+2p^2 \\ p^2-\dfrac{23p}{6}+\dfrac{19}{9} &= 0 \\ 18p^2-69p+38 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} p &= \dfrac{69\pm\sqrt{(-69)^2-4\times 18\times 38}}{2\times 18} \\ &= \dfrac{69\pm 45}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{114}{36}\text{ or }\dfrac{24}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{19}{6}\text{ or }\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
But $0\le p\le 1$ as $p$ is a probability, so
$$\therefore\ p=\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ only}$$
criteria: Correct solution, but failed to discount the invalid $p$ value

parts.latex:
A company manufactures cans of soft drink. The volume inside each can is normally distributed with a mean of 375mL and a standard deviation of 3mL. It is also known that approximately $99\%$ of the cans have a volume of less than 382mL.

During the quality control process, cans are rejected if they are underfilled or overfilled by a certain amount. $1\%$ of the cans are rejected for being underfilled and $2.5\%$ of the cans are rejected for being overfilled.

Between which two volumes do the cans that are not rejected lie?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{369_q33_s1}

$P(X<382)=0.99$ (given), and $382=375+7$, so by symmetry about the mean, $P(X>368)=0.99$ (as $368=375-7$). Hence $P(X\le 368)=0.01$, so $368$ is the minimum acceptable volume.

$369$ and $381$ are $2$ standard deviations either side of the mean ($375\pm 2\times 3$), so by the empirical rule $P(369\le X\le 381)=0.95$.

Hence $P(X<369\text{ or }X>381)=0.05$, so by symmetry $P(X>381)=0.025$, and $381$ is the maximum acceptable volume.
$$\therefore\ \text{the cans that are not rejected lie between }368\text{ mL and }381\text{ mL}$$
criteria: Finds either the upper limit or the lower limit, with working
Finds the $z$-score of $382$, or otherwise demonstrates some understanding of the normal distribution

parts.latex: Find the values of $k$, $b$ and $c$.

Passengers will have a view of the ocean when the carriage pod reaches a height of 85 metres or greater above ground.

Thilara boards the carriage pod at 12.30pm, hoping to see the ocean as much as possible before exiting the carriage pod at 1.30pm.

At what times of the day will Thilara be able to see the ocean?

solutions.latex:
The wheel has radius $50$ m and its lowest point is $10$ m above the ground, so the height ranges from $10$ m to $110$ m. The amplitude is $50$ and the centre line is $60$, so $c=60$.

One rotation takes $30$ minutes, so the period is $30$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{b} &= 30 \\ 2\pi &= 30b \\ b &= \dfrac{\pi}{15} \end{aligned}$$
The pod starts at the lowest point, a minimum, and $\cos$ starts at its maximum, so $k$ is negative: $k=-50$.

\exfigure{369_q34_s1}
$$\therefore\ k=-50,\quad b=\dfrac{\pi}{15},\quad c=60$$

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} 85 &= 60-50\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right), \quad 0\le t\le 60 \\ 25 &= -50\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right) \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right) &= -\dfrac{1}{2}, \quad 0\le\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\le 4\pi \\ \dfrac{\pi t}{15} &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3} \\ t &= 10,\ 20,\ 40,\ 50 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
At a bus stop on a particular day, a bus arrives every 10 minutes. The time spent waiting for the next bus ($X$ minutes) is a continuous random variable with the probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k & x\in[0,10]\\ 0 & x\in(-\infty,0)\cup(10,\infty)\end{cases}$$

What is the probability that at least one of his buses will require a wait time of more than 7 minutes?

solutions.latex:
The total area under the probability density function is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10k &= 1 \\ k &= 0.1 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{369_q35_s1}

$P(X>7)$ is a rectangle of width $3$ and height $0.1$:
$$P(X>7)=3\times 0.1=0.3$$
For two independent trips:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one wait is more than }7) &= 1-P(\text{neither wait is more than }7) \\ &= 1-P(\text{both waits are at most }7) \\ &= 1-\big[P(X\le 7)\big]^2 \\ &= 1-0.7^2 \\ &= 0.51 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the probability of one bus wait time being more (or less) than $7$ minutes

figures.cap: graph of y=x^2-1 from x=0 to x=k with the region below the axis and the region above the axis shaded

solutions.latex:
The two shaded areas are equal, so over $0\le x\le k$ the area below the $x$-axis cancels the area above it, and the integral is zero:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k\left(x^2-1\right)dx &= 0 \\ \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_0^k &= 0 \\ \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k &= 0 \\ k^3-3k &= 0 \\ k\left(k^2-3\right) &= 0 \\ k &= 0,\ \pm\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
But $k>1$, so $k=0$ and $k=-\sqrt{3}$ are rejected.
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt{3}$$
Alternative solution: the area below the axis, from $0$ to $1$, equals the area above it, from $1$ to $k$:
$$\begin{aligned} \left|\int_0^1\left(x^2-1\right)dx\right| &= \int_1^k\left(x^2-1\right)dx \\ \left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_0^1\right| &= \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_1^k \\ \left|\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right| &= \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right) \\ \dfrac{2}{3} &= \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k+\dfrac{2}{3} \\ \dfrac{k^3}{3}-k &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
This is the same equation as before, so $k=\sqrt{3}$.
criteria: Writes a correct equation involving integrals, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Note: you had to justify why $k$ is not $0$ or $-\sqrt{3}$.
meta.top_criterion_original: Correct solution; 1st mark for writing a correct equation involving integrals; 2nd mark for integrating $x^2-1$; 3rd mark for finding the value of $k$.

parts.latex:
An arithmetic and geometric sequence both have first term 1, and their second terms are equal.

The 14$^{\text{th}}$ term of the arithmetic sequence is three times the third term of the geometric sequence.

Given that both sequences contain only integers, find the common ratio and common difference for each sequence.

solutions.latex:
The arithmetic sequence is $1,\ 1+d,\ 1+2d,\ \ldots$ and the geometric sequence is $1,\ r,\ r^2,\ \ldots$

The second terms are equal, so $r=1+d$.

The $14^{\text{th}}$ term of the arithmetic sequence is $1+13d$, and the $3^{\text{rd}}$ term of the geometric sequence is $r^2$, so $1+13d=3r^2$.

Substitute $r=1+d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1+13d &= 3(1+d)^2 \\ 1+13d &= 3+6d+3d^2 \\ 3d^2-7d+2 &= 0 \\ (3d-1)(d-2) &= 0 \\ d &= \dfrac{1}{3}\text{ or }2 \end{aligned}$$
If $d=\dfrac{1}{3}$, the arithmetic sequence has non-integer terms (for example the second term is $\dfrac{4}{3}$), so $d=2$, and $r=1+2=3$.
$$\therefore\ \text{arithmetic: }d=2;\quad\text{geometric: }r=3$$
criteria: Solves simultaneously to obtain the two values of $r$ or $d$
Correctly uses one of the sequence formulas, for example obtains $T_2=1+d$

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct solution; 1st mark for correctly using one of the series formulas, e.g. obtaining $T_2=1+d$; 2nd mark for obtaining both equations connecting $r$ and $d$; 3rd mark for solving simultaneously to obtain the two values of $r$ or $d$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Source line read '$1+13d=r^2$' for the second condition; the question says the 14th term is THREE times the 3rd term, so it is $1+13d=3r^2$ (the source's next line, $1+13d=3(1+d)^2$, already uses this). Checked: $d=2$, $r=3$ gives $27=3\times 9$.

parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $f(x) = \log_{10}(x-1)$?

solutions.latex:
The logarithm is defined only when its argument is positive:
$$\begin{aligned} x-1 &> 0 \\ x &> 1 &&(\text{add }1) \end{aligned}$$
So the domain is $(1,\infty)$.

parts.latex: How many solutions are there to the equation $|x+1| = \sin x$ ?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{463_q2_s1}

$|x+1|\ge 0$ and $\sin x\le 1$, so a solution needs $|x+1|=\sin x\le 1$, which means $-2\le x\le 0$, and $\sin x\ge 0$.

On $-2\le x\le 0$, $\sin x\le 0$, with $\sin x=0$ only at $x=0$. But at $x=0$, $|x+1|=1\ne 0$.

So the graphs of $y=|x+1|$ and $y=\sin x$ never meet: there are no solutions.

1822.stem:
Light intensity is measured in lux. The light intensity, $I$ lux, a distance $d$ metres below the surface of the lake is given by:

$$I=6000e^{-kd}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex:
The light intensity 6 metres below the surface of the lake is 1000 lux.

Find the value of $k$, correct to four decimal places.
At what rate, in lux per metre, is the light density decreasing 6 metres below the surface of the lake, correct to the nearest lux?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $d=6$ and $I=1000$ into $I=6000e^{-kd}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000 &= 6000e^{-6k} \\ \dfrac{1}{6} &= e^{-6k} \\ \dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{6}}{-6} &= k \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=0.29862\ldots=0.2986\text{ (4 d.p.)}$$

The rate of change of the intensity is $\dfrac{dI}{dd}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dd} &= -0.2986\times 6000e^{-0.2986d} \\ &= -0.2986I \end{aligned}$$
When $d=6$, $I=1000$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dd} &= -0.2986\times 1000 \\ &= -298.6 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $-0.2986\times 6000\times e^{-0.2986\times 6}=-298.6$.

So the intensity is decreasing at about $299$ lux per metre.

parts.latex: If $\log_a 4=p$ and $\log_a 3=q$, find a simplified expression for $\log_a \dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{a}$ in terms of $p$ and $q$.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log_a\dfrac{m}{n}=\log_a m-\log_a n$, $\log_a m^k=k\log_a m$ and $\log_a a=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{a} &= \log_a\sqrt{12}-\log_a a \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_a(4\times 3)-1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\log_a 4+\log_a 3\right]-1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(p+q)-1 \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Or equivalent.

parts.latex:
The motion of a particle moving in a horizontal line is given by $x=5t\,e^{-3t}$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle in cm and $t$ is the time in minutes.

Determine the time when the particle is at rest.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when the velocity is zero. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=5t & v&=e^{-3t}\\ u'&=5 & v'&=-3e^{-3t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 5e^{-3t}+5t\left(-3e^{-3t}\right) \\ &= 5e^{-3t}-15te^{-3t} \\ &= 5e^{-3t}(1-3t) \end{aligned}$$
$v=0$ needs $5e^{-3t}(1-3t)=0$. Since $5e^{-3t}\ne 0$ for all $t$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-3t &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest after $\dfrac{1}{3}$ minute (or $20$ seconds).

1826.stem:
The function $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=(2x+1)^2$ undergoes the following \textbf{ordered} transformations to give a new function $y=g(x)$:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Horizontal translation 1 unit to the left
\item Horizontal dilation with scale factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$
\item Vertical dilation with scale factor $-4$
\item Vertical translation down 1 unit

\end{enumerate}

parts.latex: Write down the equation of the transformed function $y=g(x)$.
Write down the coordinates of the vertex of $y=g(x)$.

solutions.latex:
Apply the transformations in order, starting from $y=(2x+1)^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= (2x+1)^2 \\ y &= \left[2(x+1)+1\right]^2 = (2x+3)^2 &&(\text{translate }1\text{ unit left: replace }x\text{ with }x+1) \\ y &= \left[2(2x)+3\right]^2 = (4x+3)^2 &&(\text{horizontal dilation, factor }\dfrac{1}{2}\text{: replace }x\text{ with }2x) \\ y &= -4(4x+3)^2 &&(\text{vertical dilation, factor }-4\text{: multiply by }-4) \\ y &= -4(4x+3)^2-1 &&(\text{translate }1\text{ unit down: subtract }1) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g(x)=-4(4x+3)^2-1$$

meta.marker_note: Or equivalent.

solutions.latex:
The vertex of $g(x)=-4(4x+3)^2-1$ is where the squared bracket is zero:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x+3 &= 0 \\ x &= -\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=-1$, so the vertex is $\left(-\dfrac{3}{4},-1\right)$.

parts.latex:
The function $f(x)=\sin x$ is transformed to $g(x)=\sin\dfrac{x}{2}+1$.

Describe in words how both the period and range change in this transformation.

solutions.latex:
The period is doubled, from $2\pi$ to $4\pi$.

The range changes from $-1\le y\le 1$ to $0\le y\le 2$.

parts.latex:
Solve the equation:

$$\tan\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\quad\text{in the domain }0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

solutions.latex:
Find the range of $x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ from the range of $x$, one operation per line:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &\le x\le 2\pi \\ \dfrac{\pi}{6} &\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{13\pi}{6} &&(\text{add }\dfrac{\pi}{6}) \end{aligned}$$
$\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and tangent has period $\pi$, so
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{\pi}{6} &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6} \\ x &= 0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Solve for $x$:

$$\log_a x+\log_a(x+4)=\log_a 5$$

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms need $x>0$. Using the log law $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a mn$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a x(x+4) &= \log_a 5 \\ x(x+4) &= 5 \\ x^2+4x-5 &= 0 \\ (x+5)(x-1) &= 0 \\ x &= -5\text{ or }1 \end{aligned}$$
But $x\ne -5$ as $x>0$, so $x=1$ only.

1831.stem:
The rise and fall in sea level at Beachy Bay, due to tides, can be modelled the by the function

$$h(t)=3\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+13$$

where $h$ is the depth of the water and $t$ is the number of hours after 4am.

figures.cap: blank axes for sketching h(t)
solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of h(t) with line h=11

parts.latex:
On the set of axes below, sketch the function $h(t)$ for values $0\le t\le 24$.

\exfigure{463_q16_1}

A family wishes to spend some time at Beachy Bay, and so there is enough space on the sand they wish to go when the water depth is at most 11 metres.

Between what times \textbf{in the morning} should the family plan to be at Beachy Bay, correct to the nearest minute?

solutions.latex:
The function is $h(t)=3\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+13$, so the amplitude is $3$ and the centre line is $h=13$.

The period is given by
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &=12\end{aligned}$$
So $h$ has maximum $16$ and minimum $10$, and completes two cycles for $0\le t\le 24$.

\exfigure{463_q16_s1}

meta.format_note: Needs drawn solution: the sketch is kept as \exfigure{463_q16_s1}; source gave only the period (12) and the figure.

solutions.latex:
The depth is at most $11$ m when $h(t)\le 11$. First solve $h(t)=11$.
$$\begin{aligned}3\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+13&=11 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}&=-\dfrac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}\approx 0.8411$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants. For the first cycle, $0\le t\le 12$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{6}&\approx \pi-0.8411,\ \pi+0.8411 \\ &\approx 2.3005,\ 3.9827 \\ t&\approx 4.394,\ 7.606 \\ &\approx 4\text{ h }24\text{ min},\ 7\text{ h }36\text{ min}\end{aligned}$$
Since $t$ is the number of hours after 4 am, add 4 hours:
$$\begin{aligned}4{:}24+4\text{ h}&=8{:}24\text{ am} \\ 7{:}36+4\text{ h}&=11{:}36\text{ am}\end{aligned}$$
Between these times $\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\le-\dfrac{2}{3}$, so $h\le 11$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the family can be at the beach from } 8{:}24\text{ am until } 11{:}36\text{ am}$$

parts.latex: Which inequality gives the range of $y=x^2-6x$?

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=x^2-6x$ is an upward parabola, so $y$ has a minimum at the vertex.

Vertex: $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=\dfrac{6}{2}=3$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3^2-6\times 3 \\ &=-9\end{aligned}$$
The minimum value is $-9$, so the range is $y\ge -9$.

solutions.latex:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(x^2-5)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2-5}$$

parts.latex: Given $x+\dfrac{1}{x}=4$, what is $x^2+\dfrac{1}{x^2}$?

solutions.latex:
Squaring $x+\dfrac{1}{x}$ gives $x^2+2+\dfrac{1}{x^2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned}x^2+\dfrac{1}{x^2}&=\left(x+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^2-2 \\ &=4^2-2 \\ &=14\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: $\left(\dfrac{\sin(180^\circ-\theta)}{\sin(90^\circ-\theta)}\right)^2$ can be written as:

solutions.latex:
Using $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$, $\sin(90^\circ-\theta)=\cos\theta$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\dfrac{\sin(180^\circ-\theta)}{\sin(90^\circ-\theta)}\right)^2&=\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &=\tan^2\theta \\ &=\sec^2\theta-1\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The domain of the function $f(x)$ is $[-2,\infty)$.

What is the domain of the function $3f(-2x)-4$?

solutions.latex:
For $3f(-2x)-4$ to be defined, $-2x$ must lie in the domain of $f$, so $-2x\ge -2$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2x&\ge -2 \\ x&\le 1 &&(\text{divide by } -2 \text{, reversing the inequality})\end{aligned}$$
The vertical dilation by $3$ and the translation down $4$ do not change the domain, so the domain is $(-\infty,1]$.

parts.latex: If $\log_b 3=x$ and $\log_b 4=y$, which expression is equivalent to $\log_b(36b)$?

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log_b(AB)=\log_b A+\log_b B$ and $\log_b A^n=n\log_b A$, and $\log_b b=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_b(36b)&=\log_b 36+\log_b b \\ &=\log_b(3^2\times 4)+1 \\ &=2\log_b 3+\log_b 4+1 \\ &=2x+y+1\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the gradient of the normal to the curve $y=x^3-5x$ at $x=3$?

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is $y'$, and the gradient of the normal is $-\dfrac{1}{y'}$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3x^2-5 \\ y'(3)&=3\times 3^2-5 \\ &=22\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient of the normal}=-\dfrac{1}{22}$$

options.label: D
options.latex: Neither an odd or even function

parts.latex: Which of the following is true for the function $f(x)=\dfrac{4}{x^3}-2$?

solutions.latex:
An even function has $f(-x)=f(x)$ and an odd function has $f(-x)=-f(x)$. Test $f(-x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=\dfrac{4}{(-x)^3}-2 \\ &=-\dfrac{4}{x^3}-2 \\ &=-\left(\dfrac{4}{x^3}+2\right)\end{aligned}$$
This is not equal to $f(x)=\dfrac{4}{x^3}-2$, and not equal to $-f(x)=-\dfrac{4}{x^3}+2$.

So $f$ is neither odd nor even.

options.label: B
options.latex: $g(f(x))$ has at least two vertical asymptotes

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be an odd, continuous function with domain $(-\infty,\infty)$ and range $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Let $g(x)$ be an even rational function with vertical asymptotes only at $x=-1$ and $x=1$.

Which of the following MUST be true about $g(f(x))$?

solutions.latex:
$g$ has vertical asymptotes only at $x=\pm 1$, so $g(f(x))$ has vertical asymptotes exactly where $f(x)=1$ or $f(x)=-1$.

$f$ is continuous with range $(-\infty,\infty)$, so $f(x)=1$ has at least one solution, $x=p$.

$f$ is odd, so $f(-p)=-f(p)=-1$. Since $f(p)\ne f(-p)$, the points $x=p$ and $x=-p$ are different, so there are at least two vertical asymptotes.

There could be more than two ($f$ may reach $\pm 1$ more than once), and nothing is said about horizontal asymptotes, so only B must be true.

parts.latex: Solve $\tan^2 x=3$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
$\tan^2 x=3$, so $\tan x=\pm\sqrt{3}$. The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, since $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\sqrt{3}$.

$\tan x$ is positive in the first and third quadrants and negative in the second and fourth, for $0\le x\le 2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan x=\sqrt{3}:\quad x&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \\ \tan x=-\sqrt{3}:\quad x&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Finds $\tan x=\pm\sqrt{3}$ and the reference angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit

1844.stem: Find the following derivatives, simplifying your answers where possible.

parts.latex: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(2x+1)$
$\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{x^2-1}\right)$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos f(x)=-f'(x)\sin f(x)$, with $f(x)=2x+1$ and $f'(x)=2$:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(2x+1)=-2\sin(2x+1)$$

Using the log law $\ln\dfrac{A}{B}=\ln A-\ln B$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln x-\ln(x^2-1)\right]&=\dfrac{1}{x}-\dfrac{2x}{x^2-1} \\ &=\dfrac{(x^2-1)-2x^2}{x(x^2-1)} \\ &=\dfrac{-1-x^2}{x(x^2-1)}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=x^2-1 \\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln w=\dfrac{w'}{w}$ for $w=\dfrac{u}{v}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{x^2-1}\right)&=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x}\times\dfrac{(x^2-1)-2x^2}{(x^2-1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{x^2-1-2x^2}{x(x^2-1)} \\ &=\dfrac{-1-x^2}{x(x^2-1)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the log laws and differentiates, or equivalent merit
Applies the log laws, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the values of $x$ for which $y=x^4-24x^2+2x-14$ is concave up.

Concave up means $y''>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=4x^3-48x+2 \\ y''&=12x^2-48\end{aligned}$$
Solve $y''>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}12x^2-48&>0 \\ 12(x-2)(x+2)&>0\end{aligned}$$
This is an upward parabola in $x$, so it is positive outside its roots $x=\pm 2$.
$$\therefore\ x<-2\ \text{ or }\ x>2$$
criteria: Finds $y''$ and states $y''>0$ for concave up, or equivalent merit

For a certain suburb the number of cars, $X$, in a household has a probability distribution as follows.

\extable{464_q16_t1}

parts.latex: From a sample of 100 households, how many of them are expected to have more than two cars?
Calculate the expected value of $X$.
Show that the standard deviation of $X$ is $1.199$.

solutions.latex:
From the table, more than two cars means $X=3,\,4$ or $5$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>2)&=0.2+0.08+0.04 \\ &=0.32\end{aligned}$$
In a sample of $100$ households, the expected number is $100\times 0.32=32$.
$$\therefore\ 32\text{ households}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source had $0.2+0.08+0.04=0.056$ and no multiplication by 100; now $0.32$ and $32$ households (table: P(3)=0.2, P(4)=0.08, P(5)=0.04).

solutions.latex:
The expected value is $E(X)=\displaystyle\sum xP(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=0\times 0.06+1\times 0.32+2\times 0.3+3\times 0.2+4\times 0.08+5\times 0.04 \\ &=0+0.32+0.6+0.6+0.32+0.2 \\ &=2.04\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
\extable{Ts2727_1}

The variance is $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$, where $E(X^2)=\displaystyle\sum x^2P(x)$ is the sum of the second row and $\mu=2.04$:
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(X)&=(0.32+1.2+1.8+1.28+1)-2.04^2 \\ &=5.6-4.1616 \\ &=1.4384\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{SD}&=\sqrt{1.4384} \\ &=1.19933\ldots \\ &\approx 1.199\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of the curve $y=x^3+6x^2+9x$, labelling the stationary points, point of inflection and the intercepts with the axes.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3x^2+12x+9 \\ 0&=3(x^2+4x+3) \\ 0&=3(x+3)(x+1) \\ x&=-3\ \text{ or }\ x=-1\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using $y''=6x+12$:
$$\begin{aligned}x=-3:\quad y&=0,\ \ y''=-6<0 &&(\text{concave down, so a maximum}) \\ x=-1:\quad y&=-4,\ \ y''=6>0 &&(\text{concave up, so a minimum})\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ maximum turning point $(-3,0)$ and minimum turning point $(-1,-4)$.

Possible point of inflection: $y''=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}6x+12&=0 \\ x&=-2\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts2731_1}

The concavity changes from down to up at $x=-2$, and $y(-2)=-8+24-18=-2$.

$\therefore$ point of inflection at $(-2,-2)$.

Intercepts: when $y=0$,
$$\begin{aligned}0&=x(x^2+6x+9) \\ &=x(x+3)^2 \\ x&=0\ \text{ or }\ x=-3\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A survey found that in a large population approximately 25% of people are left-handed.

Three people are selected at random. Find the probability that at least one of them is left-handed.

solutions.latex:
'At least one left-handed' is the complement of 'none left-handed'. The chance a person is not left-handed is $0.75$, and the three selections are independent.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least 1 left-handed})&=1-P(\text{none left-handed}) \\ &=1-0.75\times 0.75\times 0.75 \\ &=0.578125 \\ &\approx 0.578\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)=2$.

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms must be defined, so $x>0$ and $x-3>0$, that is $x>3$.
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)&=2 \\ \log_2\big(x(x-3)\big)&=2 &&(\text{add logs}) \\ x(x-3)&=2^2 \\ x^2-3x-4&=0 \\ (x-4)(x+1)&=0 \\ x&=4\ \text{ or }\ x=-1\end{aligned}$$
Since $x>3$, reject $x=-1$.
$$\therefore\ x=4$$

parts.latex: Show that $A=15$.
After 4 hours, the temperature of the liquid is 80 degrees. Show that $k=\ln\sqrt{2}$.
Find the rate at which the temperature is increasing after 4 hours.

Hence, sketch the graph $T(t)=20+15e^{\ln\sqrt{2}t}$.

\exfigure{464_q21_1}

solutions.latex:
The initial temperature is the value at $t=0$, so $T(0)=35$.
$$\begin{aligned}35&=20+Ae^{0} \\ 35&=20+A \\ A&=15\end{aligned}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
After $4$ hours $T(4)=80$, with $A=15$:
$$\begin{aligned}80&=20+15e^{4k} \\ 60&=15e^{4k} \\ 4&=e^{4k} \\ 4k&=\ln 4 \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 4\end{aligned}$$
Using the log law $n\ln a=\ln a^n$, and $4=2^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}k&=\ln 4^{\frac{1}{4}} \\ &=\ln\left(2^2\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \\ &=\ln 2^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\ln\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Solves for $k$ as $\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 4$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{kt}=ke^{kt}$ with $k=\ln\sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T'(t)&=15\ln\sqrt{2}\,e^{\ln\sqrt{2}\,t} \\ T'(4)&=15\ln\sqrt{2}\,e^{4\ln\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{4\ln\sqrt{2}}=e^{\ln(\sqrt{2})^4}=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}T'(4)&=15\ln\sqrt{2}\times 4 \\ &=60\ln\sqrt{2} \\ &=30\ln 2 \\ &\approx 20.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the temperature is increasing at about } 20.8\text{ degrees per hour}$$

1856.stem: The water at a certain beach rises and falls in a periodic pattern. The height of the water at any time can be modelled by the equation $h(t)=8+5\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)$, where $t$ is time in hours after midnight.

figures.cap: blank grid with h and t axes for the sketch
solution sketch: hand sketch of h(t) over 0 to 24

parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of $y=h(t)$ for $0\le t\le 24$.

\exfigure{464_q25_1}
At what rate does the height of water change at 8:00 am? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

A boat with a depth of 5.5 metres, is scheduled to arrive at the beach at 10:00 am one day.

Explain if the boat will be able to dock.
On each day, between what times will the boat in part (c) be able to dock?

solutions.latex:
For $h(t)=8+5\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{12}$, the amplitude is $5$ and the centre line is $h=8$, so the maximum is $13$ and the minimum is $3$.

The period is
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{12}} \\ &=24\end{aligned}$$
So there is one full cycle for $0\le t\le 24$.

\exfigure{464_q25_s1}
criteria: Finds the period, amplitude or centre line, or equivalent merit

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks
meta.format_note: Needs drawn solution: sketch kept as \exfigure{464_q25_s1} (source crop). Source rubric empty; rows written from the 2 marks.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change of height is $h'(t)$.
$$\begin{aligned}h'(t)&=5\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{12} \\ &=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\end{aligned}$$
$8{:}00$ am is $t=8$ (calculator in radians):
$$\begin{aligned}h'(8)&=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\cos\dfrac{8\pi}{12} \\ &=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{5\pi}{24} \\ &\approx -0.65\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the height is decreasing at } 0.65\text{ m/h}$$

solutions.latex:
The boat arrives at $10$ am, so $t=10$.
$$\begin{aligned}h(10)&=8+5\sin\dfrac{10\pi}{12} \\ &=8+5\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=10.5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The water is $10.5$ m deep, which is more than the boat's depth of $5.5$ m, so the boat will be able to dock.

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
The boat can dock when the water is at least $5.5$ m deep, that is $h(t)\ge 5.5$. First solve $h(t)=5.5$.
$$\begin{aligned}5.5&=8+5\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{12} \\ -2.5&=5\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{12} \\ -0.5&=\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\end{aligned}$$
For $0\le t\le 24$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\le 2\pi$, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{12}&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \\ t&=14,\ 22\end{aligned}$$
$h(t)\ge 5.5$ for $0\le t\le 14$ and for $22\le t\le 24$ (for example $h(0)=8$). Here $t=14$ is $2$ pm and $t=22$ is $10$ pm.
$$\therefore\ \text{the boat can dock between } 12\text{ am and } 2\text{ pm, and between } 10\text{ pm and } 12\text{ am}$$

1857.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line and its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by:

$$v=2-\dfrac{4}{t+1}$$

parts.latex: Determine the initial velocity.
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=1$.
Find an expression for the acceleration of the particle at time $t$.
Explain why the force is always to the right for all $t\ge 0$.
Describe the motion of the particle as $t\to\infty$.

solutions.latex:
The initial velocity is at $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v(0)&=2-\dfrac{4}{0+1} \\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{initial velocity }2\text{ m/s to the left}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2-\dfrac{4}{t+1} \\ \dfrac{4}{t+1}&=2 \\ t+1&=2 \\ t&=1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest when $t=1$.

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Write $v=2-4(t+1)^{-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt} \\ &=4(t+1)^{-2} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{(t+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
The force acts in the direction of the acceleration ($F=ma$ with $m>0$), so look at the sign of $a=\dfrac{4}{(t+1)^2}$.

The numerator $4>0$, and for $t\ge 0$ the denominator $(t+1)^2\ge 1>0$ (a perfect square with minimum value $1$).

$\therefore a>0$ for all $t\ge 0$, so the force is always to the right.

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{4}{t+1}\to 0$, so $v\to 2$.

The particle is initially moving to the left, stops after $1$ second and then continues to the right, increasing in speed and approaching $2$ m/s.
criteria: States that $v\to 2$ as $t\to\infty$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is a graph of a one-to-many function?

solutions.latex:
A one-to-many relation has some $x$-value with more than one $y$-value, so a vertical line cuts its graph more than once.

Graph A is a parabola opening to the left: a vertical line to the left of the origin cuts it twice, but every horizontal line cuts it only once, so it is one-to-many.

Graph B is cut by every vertical line and every horizontal line at most once, so it is one-to-one.

Graph C is cut by every vertical line once, but a horizontal line can cut it many times, so it is many-to-one.

Graph D (a circle) is cut twice by some vertical lines and by some horizontal lines, so it is many-to-many.

Hence graph A is the one-to-many graph.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int 3^{(6x+5)}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
For an exponential $a^{f(x)}$ the rule is
$$\int f'(x)\,a^{f(x)}\,dx=\dfrac{a^{f(x)}}{\ln a}+C$$
Here $f(x)=6x+5$, so $f'(x)=6$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int 3^{6x+5}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{6}\int 6\times 3^{6x+5}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{3^{6x+5}}{\ln 3}+C \\ &=\dfrac{3^{6x+5}}{6\ln 3}+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\dfrac{3x+2}{5}-\dfrac{1-2x}{3}=8$.

Write both fractions over the common denominator $15$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{3x+2}{5}-\dfrac{1-2x}{3}&=8 \\ \dfrac{3(3x+2)-5(1-2x)}{15}&=8 \\ 9x+6-5+10x&=120 \\ 19x+1&=120 \\ 19x&=119 \\ x&=\dfrac{119}{19}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $\dfrac{12+\sqrt{32}}{3\sqrt{2}}=a+b\sqrt{2}$. Show that $a=\dfrac{4}{3}$ and $b=2$.

solutions.latex:
Simplify $\sqrt{32}=4\sqrt{2}$, then rationalise the denominator by multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{12+\sqrt{32}}{3\sqrt{2}}&=\dfrac{12+4\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{12+4\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{2}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{12\sqrt{2}+8}{6} \\ &=2\sqrt{2}+\dfrac{4}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore a=\dfrac{4}{3}$ and $b=2$.
