1872.stem:
The probability that Darcy wants to play with a football outside on any particular day is $P(F)$. The probability that it rains on any particular day is $P(R)$.

It is given that $P(F)=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $P(F\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(F'\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram of F and R with 1/4 outside, 1/2 in F only, 1/6 in the overlap

parts.latex: Is Darcy wanting to play with a football outside independent from whether or not it is raining? Justify your answer.
Given that these probabilities stay the same every day, how many days would it take to ensure a 98% chance of Darcy wanting to play football at least once?

solutions.latex:
From the given values, $P(F)=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $P(F')=\dfrac{1}{3}$, $P(F\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(F'\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

\exfigure{388_q15_s1}

Find $P(F\cap R)$ and $P(R)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(F\cap R)&=P(F)-P(F\cap R') \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(R')&=P(F\cap R')+P(F'\cap R')=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4} \\ P(R)&=1-\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Events are independent if $P(F\cap R)=P(F)\times P(R)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{6}=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Darcy wanting to play football outside is independent of the weather.
criteria: Calculates the additional probabilities, or equivalent merit

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source also gave a second 'check', $P(F\cup R)=P(F)+P(R)-P(F\cap R)$ ($\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4}$). That identity holds for any two events, so it does not test independence; removed. The independence test $P(F\cap R)=P(F)P(R)$ is unchanged.
meta.format_note: Needs drawn solution: Venn diagram kept as \exfigure{388_q15_s1} (hand-drawn source crop; values F only 1/2, F and R 1/6, neither 1/4 checked).

solutions.latex:
The days are independent, so the chance of no football on any of $n$ days is $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n$. Require at least one football day with probability $0.98$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n&=0.98 \\ \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n&=0.02 \\ n&=\dfrac{\log 0.02}{\log\frac{1}{3}} &&(\text{take logs}) \\ &=3.56\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$n$ must be a whole number of days and the chance must be at least $98\%$, so round up.
$$\therefore\ n=4\text{ days}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $1-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^n=0.98$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+1)^4$.
Hence, find $\displaystyle\int 4x^2(x^3+1)^3\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[f(x)\big]^n=n\big[f(x)\big]^{n-1}f'(x)$ with $f(x)=x^3+1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+1)^4&=4(x^3+1)^3\times 3x^2 \\ &=12x^2(x^3+1)^3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the chain rule to find the factor $4(x^3+1)^3$, or equivalent merit

1874.stem:
On any given night, the number $X$ of times that Isaac wakes up is a random variable with probability distribution given by:

\extable{388_q17_t1}

parts.latex: Show that Isaac’s parents should expect him to wake up $1.86$ times a night.
Calculate the standard deviation, correct to one decimal place.
Find the probability that Isaac wakes up greater than the expected number of times for three days in a row.

solutions.latex:
The expected value is $E(X)=\displaystyle\sum xP(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=(0\times 0.05)+(1\times 0.3)+(2\times 0.42)+(3\times 0.2)+(4\times 0.03) \\ &=0+0.3+0.84+0.6+0.12 \\ &=1.86\end{aligned}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
Using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=1.86$:
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(X)&=0^2\times 0.05+1^2\times 0.3+2^2\times 0.42+3^2\times 0.2+4^2\times 0.03-1.86^2 \\ &=4.26-3.4596 \\ &=0.8004\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma&=\sqrt{0.8004} \\ &=0.8946\ldots \\ &\approx 0.9\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\displaystyle\sum(x-\mu)^2P(x)$, where $(x-\mu)^2=3.4596,\ 0.7396,\ 0.0196,\ 1.2996,\ 4.5796$ for $x=0,1,2,3,4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(X)&=3.4596\times 0.05+0.7396\times 0.3+0.0196\times 0.42+1.2996\times 0.2+4.5796\times 0.03 \\ &=0.8004 \\ \sigma&=\sqrt{0.8004}\approx 0.9\end{aligned}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks
meta.format_note: Source rubric empty; rows written from the 2 marks.

solutions.latex:
The expected number is $1.86$, so waking more than $1.86$ times means $X\ge 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>1.86)&=P(X\ge 2) \\ &=0.42+0.2+0.03 \\ &=0.65\end{aligned}$$
The three nights are independent, so multiply:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{3 nights in a row})&=0.65^3 \\ &=0.274625 \\ &\approx 0.275\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{probability}\approx 0.275$$

figures.cap: bearing diagram C to L (3 km, 60 degrees) to R (2 km, bearing 110), north arrows at C, L and R, NOT TO SCALE
solution sketch: bearing diagram with angles 120, 130, 70, theta and the return distance x from R to C

solutions.latex:
At $L$, the angle between the north line and $LC$ is $180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$ (co-interior angles), and $LR$ is on a bearing of $110^\circ$. So $\angle CLR=360^\circ-120^\circ-110^\circ=130^\circ$.

Let $CR=x$. By the cosine rule in $\triangle CLR$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2&=3^2+2^2-2\times 3\times 2\cos 130^\circ \\ &=20.71\ldots \\ x&=4.55\text{ km} &&(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Let $\theta=\angle LRC$. By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{3}&=\dfrac{\sin 130^\circ}{x} \\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3\sin 130^\circ}{x}\right) &&(\theta \text{ acute, as } \angle L \text{ is obtuse}) \\ &\approx 30.3^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The angle between north and $RL$ at $R$ is $180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ$, so the bearing of $L$ from $R$ is $360^\circ-70^\circ=290^\circ$. $C$ is $\theta$ anticlockwise from $L$, so the bearing from $R$ to $C$ is $290^\circ-30.3^\circ\approx 260^\circ$ (or S$80^\circ$W).
$$\therefore\ \text{Henry must walk } 4.55\text{ km on a bearing of } 260^\circ$$
\exfigure{388_q18_s1}
criteria: Finds $CR=4.55$ km and the angle $\angle LRC$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=\dfrac{x^4}{x-6}$ at the point $(2,-4)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x^4 & v&=x-6 \\ u'&=4x^3 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{4x^3(x-6)-x^4}{(x-6)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{3x^4-24x^3}{(x-6)^2}\end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$ the gradient is
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{3(2)^4-24(2)^3}{(2-6)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{-144}{16} \\ &=-9\end{aligned}$$
The tangent at $(2,-4)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-y_1&=m(x-x_1) \\ y+4&=-9(x-2) \\ y+4&=-9x+18 \\ y&=-9x+14 \\ 9x+y-14&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit

The boundary values are $k^2=64$, so $k=\pm 8$. As a graph in $k$, $k^2-64$ is an upward parabola, which is $\ge 0$ outside its roots.

$$\therefore\ k\le -8\ \text{ or }\ k\ge 8$$

1881.stem: The graph of the function $f(x)=x^3$ is translated up 9 units, left 4 units, then dilated vertically by a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$, to make a new graph, $g(x)$.

parts.latex: Find the equation, $g(x)$, of the new graph.

A point $P(a,b)$ on $f(x)$ is transformed to the point $Q(-1,12)$ on $g(x)$.

Find the values of $a$ and $b$.

solutions.latex:
Apply the transformations to $f(x)=x^3$ in the order given:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)+9&=x^3+9 &&(\text{translate up } 9) \\ f(x+4)+9&=(x+4)^3+9 &&(\text{translate left } 4) \\ \dfrac{1}{3}\big[f(x+4)+9\big]&=\dfrac{1}{3}\big[(x+4)^3+9\big] &&(\text{dilate vertically, scale factor } \dfrac{1}{3})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left((x+4)^3+9\right) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}(x+4)^3+3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies two of the transformations correctly, or equivalent merit
Applies one of the transformations correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Source rubric: 1 mark for each transformation.

solutions.latex:
$Q(-1,12)$ is the image of $P(a,b)$, so undo the transformations in reverse order.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Undo the vertical dilation (multiply } y \text{ by } 3)&:\ (-1,12)\text{ becomes }(-1,36) \\ \text{Undo the translation left } 4 \text{ (add } 4 \text{ to } x)&:\ (-1,36)\text{ becomes }(3,36) \\ \text{Undo the translation up } 9 \text{ (subtract } 9 \text{ from } y)&:\ (3,36)\text{ becomes }(3,27)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=3,\ b=27$$
criteria: Finds one of $a$ or $b$ with working, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 mark for each value of $a$ and $b$ showing working
meta.marker_note: Source rubric: 1 mark for each value of $a$ and $b$, showing working.

parts.latex:
The difference in sound levels in decibels (dB) can be modelled by the equation

$$D_2-D_1=10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I_2}{I_1}\right)$$

Where $D_1$ and $D_2$ are the sound levels and $I_1$ and $I_2$ are their respective sound intensities measured in watts/m$^2$.

A conversation has a sound level of $60$ dB. A vacuum cleaner has an intensity that is $100$ times more than the conversation. Calculate the sound level of the vacuum cleaner.

solutions.latex:
Let $D_1=60$ and $I_2=100I_1$:
$$\begin{aligned}D_2-60&=10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{100I_1}{I_1}\right) \\ &=10\log_{10}100 \\ &=10\times 2 \\ &=20 \\ D_2&=80\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the sound level is } 80\text{ dB}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $D_2-60=10\log_{10}100$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct use of log law and final solution

parts.latex: Given $2\log_4 y-\log_4 8+\log_4 x=2$, show that $y=\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{x}}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $n\log_4 a=\log_4 a^n$, $\log_4 a-\log_4 b=\log_4\dfrac{a}{b}$ and $\log_4 a+\log_4 b=\log_4 ab$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\log_4 y-\log_4 8+\log_4 x&=2 \\ \log_4\left(\dfrac{y^2x}{8}\right)&=2 \\ \dfrac{y^2x}{8}&=4^2 \\ y^2x&=128 \\ y^2&=\dfrac{128}{x} \\ y&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{128}}{\sqrt{x}} \\ &=\pm\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}$$
Since $\log_4 y$ is defined, $y>0$, so
$$y=\dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{x}}$$
criteria: Works towards $y$ as the subject, or equivalent merit
Simplifies the logarithms, or equivalent merit

1884.stem:
Anubhav is doing some research on the number of patients emergency waiting rooms across all NSW hospitals at any given time. He notices that the number of patients, $P$, can be modelled by the function $M(t)=a\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+b$, where $t$ is the time since 12 am. The maximum number of patients is $2500$ and the minimum is $700$. The graph of $P(t)$ is shown below.

\exfigure{388_q27_1}

figures.cap: graph of P(t): cosine curve from 2500 at t=0 down to a minimum of 700 and back up to 2500 at t=c

parts.latex: What are the values of $a$ and $b$ in the equation and $c$ on the graph?
Between what times (to the nearest minute) each day are there less than $1000$ patients in emergency waiting rooms across all NSW hospitals?

solutions.latex:
The graph is a cosine curve starting at its maximum $2500$, with minimum $700$.
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{2500-700}{2}=900 &&(\text{amplitude}) \\ b&=\dfrac{2500+700}{2}=1600 &&(\text{centre line})\end{aligned}$$
$c$ is the end of one full period:
$$\begin{aligned}c&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &=12\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=900,\ b=1600,\ c=12$$
criteria: Finds two of $a$, $b$ and $c$, or equivalent merit
Finds one of $a$, $b$ and $c$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Source rubric: 1 mark for each variable.
meta.source_flag: The question names the function $M(t)$ but the graph axis and the text call the quantity $P(t)$ (inconsistency in the paper; question not changed).

solutions.latex:
There are fewer than $1000$ patients when $900\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+1600<1000$. First solve for equality:
$$\begin{aligned}1000&=900\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+1600 \\ -600&=900\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6} \\ -\dfrac{2}{3}&=\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}=0.841\ldots$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants. For the first period, $0\le t\le 12$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{6}&=\pi-0.841,\ \pi+0.841 \\ t&=\dfrac{6(\pi-0.841)}{\pi},\ \dfrac{6(\pi+0.841)}{\pi} \\ &=4.39\ldots,\ 7.60\ldots \\ &\approx 4{:}24,\ 7{:}36\end{aligned}$$
Between these times $\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}<-\dfrac{2}{3}$. The period is $12$ hours, so the same happens $12$ hours later.
$$\therefore\ \text{fewer than } 1000 \text{ patients between } 4{:}24\text{ am and } 7{:}36\text{ am, and between } 4{:}24\text{ pm and } 7{:}36\text{ pm}$$
criteria: Finds both values of $t$ in the first period, or equivalent merit
Finds the reference angle $0.841\ldots$, or equivalent merit

1885.stem: Carlisle is playing a game, in which he has to position a bomb anywhere on a number plane. When the bomb explodes it will kill anything within its circular blast zone.

figures.cap: solution sketch: diagram of the blast circle centre (10,-5) with the enemy at (2,-4) outside it

parts.latex: Find the position that Carlisle placed the bomb on the number plane and the radius of its circular blast zone, given its’ blast zone has an equation $x^2-20x+y^2+10y=-76$.
Determine if an enemy located at the coordinates $(2,-4)$ will be killed when the bomb explodes. Justify your decision with a diagram and/or calculations.

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$ (add $100$ and $25$ to both sides):
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-20x+100+y^2+10y+25&=-76+100+25 \\ (x-10)^2+(y+5)^2&=49 \\ (x-10)^2+(y+5)^2&=7^2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the bomb is at $(10,-5)$ and the blast zone has radius $7$ units.
criteria: Completes the square and finds the centre, or equivalent merit
Completes the square, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The enemy is killed only if its distance from the centre $(10,-5)$ is less than the radius $7$.
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\sqrt{(10-2)^2+(-5-(-4))^2} \\ &=\sqrt{8^2+(-1)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{65} \\ &=8.06\ldots\end{aligned}$$
Since $8.06>7$, the enemy is outside the blast zone and will survive.

parts.latex: Find $h(x)$, where $h(x)=f(g(x))$.
State the domain for $h(x)$.

solutions.latex:
$h(x)=f(g(x))$: replace $x$ in $f(x)=\sqrt{3x-15}$ by $g(x)=-6x-4$.
$$\begin{aligned}h(x)&=\sqrt{3(-6x-4)-15} \\ &=\sqrt{-18x-12-15} \\ &=\sqrt{-18x-27}\end{aligned}$$

The square root needs $-18x-27\ge 0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-18x-27&\ge 0 \\ -18x&\ge 27 &&(\text{add } 27) \\ x&\le -\dfrac{3}{2} &&(\text{divide by } -18 \text{, reversing the inequality})\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{domain } \left(-\infty,\,-\dfrac{3}{2}\right]$$
criteria: Identifies the domain condition, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Jacinta is gifted \$5000 from her grandmother. The money is invested for 18 years, earning 7% p.a. in interest, compounded monthly. Calculate the effective annual interest rate of the investment over the 18 years. Answer as a percentage correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Method 1: find the final amount, then the annual rate that gives the same growth over $18$ years.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=5000\left(1+\dfrac{0.07}{12}\right)^{12\times 18} \\ &=17\,562.69661\ldots \\ 17\,562.69661&=5000(1+r)^{18} \\ (1+r)^{18}&=3.512539\ldots \\ 1+r&=\sqrt[18]{3.512539}=1.072290081 \\ r&=0.072290 \\ &\approx 7.23\%\text{ (to 2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: the effective annual rate is $\text{EAR}=\left(1+\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^n-1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{EAR}&=\left(1+\dfrac{0.07}{12}\right)^{12}-1 \\ &=0.07229\ldots \\ &\approx 7.23\%\text{ (to 2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the compound interest formula, or equivalent merit

1888.stem:
Ashley borrows \$500 000 from a bank in a reducing balance loan for which she is charged an interest rate of 6% per annum, compounded monthly. At the end of each month Ashley is required to make a repayment of \$4000.

The amount in the account immediately after the $n$th repayment can be determined using the recurrence relation

$$A_n=A_{n-1}(1.005)-4000$$

where $n=1,2,3\ldots$ and $A_0=500\,000$.

parts.latex: Use the recurrence relation to determine the amount of money owing immediately after the third repayment.
Hence, find how many months it will take for Ashley to repay the \$500 000.

criteria: Finds $A_1$ and $A_2$ correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks
meta.format_note: Source rubric empty; rows written from the 2 marks. Checked: A3 = 495 477.4625.

criteria: Writes $A_n$ as $500\,000(1.005)^n$ less a sum of terms in powers of $1.005$, or equivalent merit
Finds $A_2$ or $A_3$ in terms of powers of $1.005$, or equivalent merit

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks
meta.format_note: Source rubric empty; rows written from the 3 marks.

solutions.latex:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=500\,000(1.005)^n-4000\left(\dfrac{1.005^n-1}{0.005}\right) \\ 0&=500\,000(1.005)^n-800\,000\left(1.005^n-1\right) &&(4000\div 0.005=800\,000) \\ 500\,000(1.005)^n&=800\,000\left(1.005^n-1\right) \\ 1.005^n&=1.6\left(1.005^n-1\right) &&(\text{divide by } 500\,000) \\ 1.005^n&=1.6\times 1.005^n-1.6 \\ 1.6&=1.6\times 1.005^n-1.005^n \\ 1.6&=1.005^n(1.6-1) \\ 1.005^n&=\dfrac{8}{3} \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\frac{8}{3}}{\ln 1.005} \\ &=196.6558\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$n$ is a whole number of repayments, and after $196$ repayments some of the loan is still owing, so
$$\therefore\ n=197\text{ months}$$
criteria: Sets $A_n=0$ and simplifies, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $f'(x)=3e^x\,(3x^2+x^3)$.

Find any points of inflection of $f(x)$.

(You may state the values of the points correct to 1 decimal place.)
Show that the only stationary points of $f(x)$ are $(0,0)$ and $(-3,-81e^{-3})$ and determine their nature.

Hence sketch the curve of $f(x)=3x^3\,e^x$ for $x<1$, showing any stationary points, points of inflection and intercepts with the axes.

\exfigure{388_q32_1}

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=3x^3 & v&=e^x \\ u'&=9x^2 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=9x^2e^x+3x^3e^x \\ &=3e^x\left(3x^2+x^3\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks
meta.format_note: Source rubric empty; rows written from the 2 marks.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $f'(x)=3e^x\left(3x^2+x^3\right)$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=3e^x & v&=3x^2+x^3 \\ u'&=3e^x & v'&=6x+3x^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=3e^x\left(3x^2+x^3\right)+3e^x\left(6x+3x^2\right) \\ &=9x^2e^x+3x^3e^x+18xe^x+9x^2e^x \\ &=18xe^x+18x^2e^x+3x^3e^x \\ &=3xe^x\left(6+6x+x^2\right)\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection: $f''(x)=0$, so $3xe^x\left(x^2+6x+6\right)=0$. Since $e^x>0$, either $x=0$ or $x^2+6x+6=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{36-4(1)(6)}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{12}}{2} \\ &=-3\pm\sqrt{3} \\ &\approx -1.3,\ -4.7 &&(\text{to 1 dp})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(0)&=3(0)^3e^0=0 \\ f\left(-3+\sqrt{3}\right)&\approx -1.7 \\ f\left(-3-\sqrt{3}\right)&\approx -2.8\end{aligned}$$
Test whether the concavity changes (use $f''(x)$, not gradients):

\extable{Ts2797_1}

$f''(x)$ changes sign at each of the three values of $x$: from $<0$ to $>0$ about $x=-4.7$, from $>0$ to $<0$ about $x=-1.3$, and from $<0$ to $>0$ about $x=0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{points of inflection } (0,0),\ (-1.3,-1.7)\text{ and }(-4.7,-2.8)$$
criteria: Finds $f''(x)$ and the possible points of inflection, or equivalent merit

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $f''(-1)=-3e^{-1}\approx-1.10$, not $-0.04$ (sign and conclusion unchanged).
meta.format_note: Source rubric empty; rows written from the 3 marks. Table Ts2797_1 uses $x=-1.26$ and $f''=0$ there, but the root is $-3+\sqrt3=-1.268\ldots$ (the source also wrote $-1.26\ldots$); the sign conclusion is unaffected. Source gave $f(-1.3)=-1.7$: that value is at the exact root ($f(-1.3)$ itself is $-1.8$).

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. Since $3e^x>0$, only the other factor can be zero:
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2+x^3&=0 \\ x^2(3+x)&=0 \\ x&=0\ \text{ or }\ x=-3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(0)&=3(0)^3e^0=0 \\ f(-3)&=3(-3)^3e^{-3}=-81e^{-3}\end{aligned}$$
So the only stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(-3,-81e^{-3})$.

Nature of $x=-3$, using $f''(x)=3xe^x\left(6+6x+x^2\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-3)&=3(-3)e^{-3}\left(6+6(-3)+(-3)^2\right) \\ &=27e^{-3} \\ &\approx 1.34>0 &&(\text{concave up})\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ minimum turning point at $(-3,-81e^{-3})$.

At $x=0$, $f''(0)=0$, so test the gradient either side:

\extable{Ts2798_1}

The gradient is positive on both sides of $(0,0)$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection (consistent with part (b)).
criteria: Finds both stationary points and the nature of $(-3,-81e^{-3})$, or equivalent merit
Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which one of the following statements about the line $12x-4y=0$ is NOT true?

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to gradient-intercept form: $4y=12x$, so $y=3x$.

parts.latex:
The parabola $f(x)=-x^2+9mx+2$ has a maximum at $x=\dfrac{2}{m}$, where $m$ is a constant such that $m\neq 0$.

What are the values of $m$?

solutions.latex:
The parabola $f(x)=-x^2+9mx+2$ has its maximum at the axis of symmetry
$$x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=-\dfrac{9m}{2(-1)}=\dfrac{9m}{2}$$
Equate this to $\dfrac{2}{m}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9m}{2} &= \dfrac{2}{m} \\ 9m^2 &= 4 \\ m &= \pm\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The parabola opens downwards for any $m$, so both values give a maximum.

meta.self_check: Solved 9m^2=4 by hand; vertex x=9m/2 checked via f'(x)=-2x+9m=0.

parts.latex: What are the coordinates of the turning point to the curve $y=e^x-ex$ ?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate: $y'=e^x-e$.

Turning point where $y'=0$: $e^x=e$, so $x=1$.

Then $y=e^1-e(1)=0$, so the turning point is $(1,0)$.

Since $y''=e^x>0$, it is a minimum.

meta.self_check: Hand calculation: y'=0 at x=1, y(1)=0.

parts.latex:
A series has following terms:

$2+5+8+11+14+17+\ldots$

What is the sum of the first 30 terms of the series

solutions.latex:
The terms increase by $3$ each time, so this is an arithmetic series with $a=2$ and $d=3$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $n=30$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{30} &= \dfrac{30}{2}\big(2(2)+29(3)\big) \\ &= 15\times 91 \\ &= 1365 \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: Kelly 1.6 m tall, 8 m from a tree of height h, bird at top

solutions.latex:
The bird is $h-1.6$ metres above Kelly's eyes. The angle of depression of Kelly from the bird is $73^\circ$, so by alternate angles the angle of elevation of the bird from Kelly's eyes is $73^\circ$.

In the right-angled triangle with horizontal side $8$ m:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 73^\circ &= \dfrac{h-1.6}{8} \\ h-1.6 &= 8\tan 73^\circ \approx 26.17 \\ h &\approx 27.77\text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Option C ($26.17$) forgets to add Kelly's height of $1.6$ m.

parts.latex:
The functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ are defined as follows:

$g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{8}$ \qquad $h(x)=\sqrt{2x}+3$

Which is the correct expression for $h(g(x))$?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)$ into $h$:
$$\begin{aligned} h(g(x)) &= \sqrt{2\cdot\dfrac{x^2}{8}}+3 \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{x^2}{4}}+3 \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2}+3 \end{aligned}$$
(taking $x\ge 0$; in general this is $\dfrac{|x|}{2}+3$, and option C is the only option of this form).

figures.cap: trigonometric graph, amplitude 3, from -2pi to 2pi

solutions.latex:
The graph has amplitude $3$, period $\pi$ and a maximum at $x=0$, so it is $y=3\cos 2x$.

Check each option:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= 3\cos 2x \\ 3\cos 2(x-\pi) &= 3\cos(2x-2\pi) = 3\cos 2x \end{aligned}$$
so B, C and D all describe the graph.

For A: $3\sin 2\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=3\sin(2x+\pi)=-3\sin 2x$, which is $0$ at $x=0$, not a maximum.

parts.latex: Solve $\log_3 5=2\log_3 10-\log_3 x$.

solutions.latex:
Rearranging so the logarithms are on one side.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_3 x &= 2\log_3 10-\log_3 5 \\ &= \log_3 10^2-\log_3 5 &&(\text{power law}) \\ &= \log_3 \dfrac{100}{5} &&(\text{quotient law}) \\ &= \log_3 20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 20$$
criteria: Applies a log law correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Find the coordinates of the centre and the radius of the circle with equation

$$x^2+8x+y^2-6y-24=0$$

solutions.latex:
Completing the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+8x+16+y^2-6y+9 &= 24+16+9 \\ (x+4)^2+(y-3)^2 &= 49 \end{aligned}$$
Comparing with $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$:
$$\therefore\ \text{centre } (-4,\,3),\quad \text{radius } 7$$
criteria: Completes the square in $x$ and $y$, or equivalent merit

The remaining cells follow from the totals ($12$ gym, $13$ run, $24$ altogether).

parts.latex: How much profit or loss would they make on a day where they sold 30 Midiens? Clearly state profit or loss.

1905.stem: The number of people ($N$) who attend a show at a venue varies inversely with the amount of floor space in cm$^2$ allowed per person ($A$). Three hundred people attended the venue when 1m$^2$ of floor space was allowed per person.

parts.latex: Find the constant ($k$) of variation.
Hence or otherwise, find how many people can attend the venue if each person is allowed 4500 cm$^2$ of floor space.

solutions.latex:
$N$ varies inversely with $A$, so $N=\dfrac{k}{A}$ with $A$ in $\text{cm}^2$.

Since $1\text{ m}^2=10\,000\text{ cm}^2$, $A=10\,000$ when $N=300$.
$$\begin{aligned} 300 &= \dfrac{k}{10\,000} \\ k &= 3\,000\,000 \end{aligned}$$

Using $N=\dfrac{3\,000\,000}{A}$ with $A=4500$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= \dfrac{3\,000\,000}{4500} \\ &= 666 \cdot \dot{6} \end{aligned}$$
Only whole people can attend, and the venue cannot exceed this, so round down.
$$\therefore\ 666 \text{ people}$$
criteria: Substitutes $A=4500$ into the formula, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: Answer 666.67 needs a rounding decision (666 rounding down because it is a maximum; 667 if rounded to nearest). Marker to confirm. If part (a) were answered with A in m^2 (k=300), 300/0.45 gives the same 666.67.

1906.stem: Consider the series $\ln x-3(\ln x)^2+9(\ln x)^3+\cdots$

parts.latex: Show that these terms form a geometric series.
Hence, or otherwise, find the values of $x$ for which the series has a limiting sum.

solutions.latex:
A series is geometric when the ratio of consecutive terms is constant.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} &= \dfrac{-3(\ln x)^2}{\ln x} = -3\ln x \\ \dfrac{T_3}{T_2} &= \dfrac{9(\ln x)^3}{-3(\ln x)^2} = -3\ln x \end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so the series is geometric with $a=\ln x$ and $r=-3\ln x$.

A geometric series has a limiting sum when $|r|<1$, with $r=-3\ln x$. The terms need $x>0$ and the series needs $\ln x\ne 0$ (for $x=1$ every term is $0$, so there is no ratio).
$$\begin{aligned} |-3\ln x| &< 1 \\ -1 &< 3\ln x < 1 \\ -\dfrac{1}{3} &< \ln x < \dfrac{1}{3} &&(\text{divide by } 3) \\ e^{-\frac{1}{3}} &< x < e^{\frac{1}{3}} &&(e^{(\cdot)} \text{ is increasing}) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ e^{-\frac{1}{3}}<x<e^{\frac{1}{3}}\quad(x\ne 1)$$
criteria: Uses $|r|<1$ with $r=-3\ln x$, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: Excluding x=1 is a judgement: the likely school answer is e^{-1/3}<x<e^{1/3} (x=1 gives a zero series, whose sum is 0). Marker to confirm whether x≠1 is required.

figures.cap: park: semicircle lake above rectangle with grassed section; measurements 135 m, 120 m, 180 m, 110 m, 220 m

parts.latex:
A landscaper, Annabel, wanted to ask the local council to renovate the park near her home. Her suggestion was to have a park partially occupied by a lake and the rest be a grassed section, as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{394_q18_1}

The park consists of a rectangle with dimensions 220 m and 180 m, and a semi-circle with a radius of 110 m. Some measurements from the end of the grassed section to the edge of the lake are also shown.

Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule, calculate the approximate area of the lake, to the nearest square metre.

solutions.latex:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule means 3 function values, so $h=\dfrac{220}{2}=110$ m. The heights of the grassed section are $135$, $120$ and $180$ m (the right end reaches the top of the rectangle).
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{grass}} &\approx \dfrac{110}{2}\big[135+2(120)+180\big] \\ &= 55\times 555 \\ &= 30\,525 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The rectangle has area $220\times 180=39\,600\text{ m}^2$, so the lake inside the rectangle is
$$39\,600-30\,525=9075\text{ m}^2$$
The semicircle (radius $110$ m) has area
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(110)^2=6050\pi\approx 19\,006.6\text{ m}^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lake} &\approx 9075+19\,006.6 \\ &\approx 28\,082 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the approximate area of the grassed section, or the lake inside the rectangle, or equivalent merit
Writes the trapezoidal rule with $h=110$ and the values $135$, $120$, $180$, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: Reading of the figure: heights 135 (left), 120 (middle), 180 (right, where the lake edge meets the top of the rectangle). The dotted line and 110 m marking are consistent with h=110. Verify against the original paper.

1908.stem: The third term in a geometric sequence 18 and the sixth term is 486.

parts.latex: Find the first term and the common ratio.
Find the sum of first 10 terms of this sequence.

solutions.latex:
Let the first term be $a$ and the common ratio $r$. Then $T_3=ar^2=18$ and $T_6=ar^5=486$.

Dividing the second equation by the first:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{ar^5}{ar^2} &= \dfrac{486}{18} \\ r^3 &= 27 \\ r &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Then $9a=18$.
$$\therefore\ a=2,\quad r=3$$
criteria: Finds $r=3$, or writes $ar^2=18$ and $ar^5=486$, or equivalent merit

meta.stem_note: Stem reads 'The third term ... 18' (missing 'is'); taken as T3=18.

parts.latex:
Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=3\log_e 2x$, when it passes through the point $P$ whose $x-$coordinate is 2. Leave your answer in the form:

$$y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $y=3\ln 2x=3\ln 2+3\ln x$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{x}$$
At $x=2$: the gradient of the tangent is $\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $y=3\ln 4$ (so $P=(2,\,3\ln 4)$).

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ y-3\ln 4=-\dfrac{2}{3}(x-2)$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal and the $y$-coordinate of $P$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_1^6 f(x)\,dx=6$ and $\displaystyle\int_3^6 f(x)\,dx=-4$. What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_1^3 \left(f(x)+x\right)dx$ ?

solutions.latex:
Splitting the interval, $\displaystyle\int_1^6 f(x)\,dx=\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx+\int_3^6 f(x)\,dx$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3 f(x)\,dx &= 6-(-4) \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
Also
$$\int_1^3 x\,dx=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^3=\dfrac{9}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}=4$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3 \big(f(x)+x\big)dx &= 10+4 \\ &= 14 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\displaystyle\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx=10$ or $\displaystyle\int_1^3 x\,dx=4$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\left(1+e^{2x}\right)^8$.

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $u=1+e^{2x}$, so $y=u^8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{du}{dx}&=2e^{2x} & \dfrac{dy}{du}&=8u^7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 8\left(1+e^{2x}\right)^7\times 2e^{2x} \\ &= 16e^{2x}\left(1+e^{2x}\right)^7 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the chain rule with a correct derivative of $u$ or $u^8$, or equivalent merit

1912.stem:
An object moves along the number line so that its displacement ($x$ metres) from the origin is given by:

$$x(t)=12-2t+12\log_e(t+3)$$

where time $t$ is measured in seconds.

parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=3$.
In which direction is the particle moving when $t>3$ ? Justify your statement with mathematical working or in words.
can_use: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Initially means $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 12-0+12\ln 3 \\ &= 12+12\ln 3 \\ &\approx 25.2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is } 12+12\ln 3\approx 25.2\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$

The particle is at rest when the velocity $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}$$
When $t=3$:
$$v=-2+\dfrac{12}{6}=0$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest when $t=3$.

For $t>3$ we have $t+3>6$, so
$$\dfrac{12}{t+3}<\dfrac{12}{6}=2 \quad\text{and hence}\quad v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}<0$$
$\therefore$ the velocity is negative, so the particle moves in the negative direction (to the left).
criteria: Shows $v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}$ and attempts to find its sign, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A}{\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A}=\sec^2A$.
Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int \tan^2x\left(\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\sin A$, using $\operatorname{cosec}A\sin A=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A\sin A}{\operatorname{cosec}A\sin A-\sin^2A} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2A} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2A} &&(\sin^2A+\cos^2A=1) \\ &= \sec^2A \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Multiplies by $\sin A$ or rewrites in terms of $\sin A$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By part (a) the bracket equals $\sec^2x$, so the integrand is $\tan^2x\sec^2x$.

Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x)=\sec^2x$, this is of the form $u^2u'$ with $u=\tan x$.
$$\int \tan^2x\sec^2x\,dx=\dfrac{\tan^3x}{3}+C$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3\dfrac{3x^2-1}{5x^3-5x+9}\,dx$ leaving your answer in simplest exact form.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator. Let $u=5x^3-5x+9$, so $du=(15x^2-5)\,dx=5(3x^2-1)\,dx$.

Limits: $x=1$ gives $u=9$; $x=3$ gives $u=135-15+9=129$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3\dfrac{3x^2-1}{5x^3-5x+9}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{5}\int_9^{129}\dfrac{du}{u} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{5}\Big[\ln u\Big]_9^{129} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{5}\ln\dfrac{129}{9} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{5}\ln\dfrac{43}{3}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly and finds the new limits, or finds $\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(5x^3-5x+9)$, or equivalent merit
Recognises the numerator as a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If $\sec^2\theta=2$ and $0\le\theta\le\pi$, find all possible values of $\theta$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sec^2\theta &= 2 \\ \cos^2\theta &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \cos\theta &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$, the related acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. $\cos\theta>0$ gives $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\cos\theta<0$ gives $\theta=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\ \text{or}\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Finds $\cos\theta=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, or one correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
$f(x)$ is transformed to $g(x)$ such that,

$$g(x)=2f(3-x)$$

Describe the three transformations in the correct order.

solutions.latex:
Completing the square is already done: the turning point is $(-2,-1)$.

$x$-intercepts: $(x+2)^2-1=0$ gives $x+2=\pm1$, so $x=-1$ or $x=-3$.

$y$-intercept: $f(0)=4-1=3$.

\exfigure{394_q27_s1}

solutions.latex:
Write $g(x)=2f\big(-(x-3)\big)$. Applying the transformations to $y=f(x)$ in order:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &\to f(-x) &&\text{reflect in the } y\text{-axis} \\ f(-x) &\to f\big(-(x-3)\big)=f(3-x) &&\text{translate 3 units right} \\ f(3-x) &\to 2f(3-x) &&\text{vertical dilation, factor } 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Describes two of the transformations correctly, or equivalent merit
Describes one transformation correctly, or equivalent merit

1917.stem:
In the diagram $\triangle AOB$ is a section of a regular ten sided decagon inscribed in a circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$ cm.

\exfigure{394_q28_1}

figures.cap: triangle AOB inside a circle, OA = OB = r cm

parts.latex: Find $r$ given that the area of the full decagon is $100\ \text{cm}^2$.
Find the perimeter of the decagon. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The decagon splits into 10 congruent isosceles triangles, each with two sides $r$ and included angle $\dfrac{360^\circ}{10}=36^\circ$ at $O$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10\times\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin 36^\circ &= 100 \\ r^2 &= \dfrac{20}{\sin 36^\circ} \\ r &= \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{\sin 36^\circ}} \\ &\approx 5.83 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the area of the decagon in terms of $r$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle AOB$, $OA=OB=r$ and $\angle AOB=36^\circ$. Using the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2 &= r^2+r^2-2r^2\cos 36^\circ \\ &= 2r^2(1-\cos 36^\circ) \\ &= 2\times 34.026(1-\cos 36^\circ) \\ AB &= 3.605\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Perimeter}=10\times AB\approx 36.051\text{ cm}$$

meta.concern: Value 36.051 uses unrounded r=5.8332 from part (a); using r=5.83 gives 36.032. Marker to use the unrounded r.

1918.stem:
The graph of $y=2e^{x+b}+c$ is given below.

\exfigure{394_q29_1}

figures.cap: exponential graph with dashed horizontal line at y = -2

parts.latex: In your own words, justify why $c=-2$.
Show that $b=1$.
Find the area bounded by the curve, the $x-$ axis and the $y-$ axis.

solutions.latex:
The curve has a horizontal asymptote, shown dashed on the graph, at $y=-2$.

As $x\to-\infty$, $e^{x+b}\to0$, so $y=2e^{x+b}+c\to c$.

Hence the asymptote is $y=c$, and therefore $c=-2$.

meta.self_check: Read asymptote y=-2 from graph; limit argument.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $c=-2$, so $y=2e^{x+b}-2$.

The graph crosses the $x$-axis at $(-1,0)$, so substitute $x=-1$, $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2e^{-1+b}-2 \\ e^{b-1} &= 1 \\ b-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b=1$$

meta.self_check: Substituting b=1 gives y(-1)=0; y(0)=2e-2~3.44 matches graph (about 3.4).

solutions.latex:
With $b=1$ and $c=-2$, the curve is $y=2e^{x+1}-2$. It lies above the $x$-axis for $-1\le x\le0$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^{0}\left(2e^{x+1}-2\right)dx \\ &= \Big[2e^{x+1}-2x\Big]_{-1}^{0} \\ &= \left(2e-0\right)-\left(2+2\right) \\ &= 2e-4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=2e-4\approx1.44 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral and primitive, or equivalent merit

Tick labels -1 (x) and 2, 3 (y) nudged along their own side off the curve; -2 raised above the dashed line. 1919.stem:
When Lucio plays for his soccer team, they have an 85% chance of winning. When he does not play, their chance of winning is 40%.

The chance that Lucio plays any particular game is 90%.

parts.latex: Find the probability that Lucio plays and his team wins.
Find the probability that Lucio played, given that his team won.

solutions.latex:
Lucio plays with probability $0.9$, and then the team wins with probability $0.85$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{plays and wins}) &= 0.9\times0.85 \\ &= 0.765 \end{aligned}$$

The team can win with Lucio playing, or without him.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{win}) &= 0.9\times0.85+0.1\times0.4 \\ &= 0.765+0.04 \\ &= 0.805 \end{aligned}$$
Using conditional probability, $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{played}\mid\text{won}) &= \dfrac{0.765}{0.805} \\ &= \dfrac{153}{161} \\ &\approx 0.950 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
In a game of chance, a player is to spin a spinner with sectors of unequal sizes.

The following table gives the probability distribution of the money that the player could win.

\extable{394_q31_t1}

The expected value of the game is \$4000.

What is the probability of winning \$6000 or more?

solutions.latex:
The probabilities add to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{5}+x+\dfrac{1}{5}+y &= 1 \\ x+y &= \dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}\qquad (1)$$
The expected value is $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2000\times\dfrac{2}{5}+4000x+6000\times\dfrac{1}{5}+8000y &= 4000 \\ 800+4000x+1200+8000y &= 4000 \\ 4000x+8000y &= 2000 \\ x+2y &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}\qquad (2)$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$y=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{2}{5}=\dfrac{1}{10}$$
Then $x=\dfrac{2}{5}-\dfrac{1}{10}=\dfrac{3}{10}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\$6000\text{ or more}) &= P(6000)+P(8000) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the expected value equation and finds one correct equation in $x$ and $y$ from it, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: E=800+1200+1200+800=4000 with x=.3,y=.1; probabilities sum to 1.

1921.stem:
An open topped fish tank of volume 30 m$^3$ is to be made in the shape of a rectangular prism with length $3x$ metres, width $x$ metres and height $h$ metres.

Materials cost \$20 per square metre for the base of the tank and \$35 per square metre for the sides of the tank.

parts.latex:
Show that the total cost \$$C$ of making the fish tank is given by

$$C=60x^2+\dfrac{2800}{x}$$
Hence find the dimensions of such a tank with the least total cost. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The volume is $30$ m$^3$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 3x\cdot x\cdot h &= 30 \\ h &= \dfrac{10}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
The base has area $3x\cdot x=3x^2$ and the four sides (open top) have area $2(3x\cdot h)+2(x\cdot h)=8xh$.
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 20\times3x^2+35\times8xh \\ &= 60x^2+280x\times\dfrac{10}{x^2} \\ &= 60x^2+\dfrac{2800}{x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the base and of the sides and substitutes into the cost, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: Numerical: at x=2.8575 C=1469.8 from both forms.

solutions.latex:
Minimise $C=60x^2+2800x^{-1}$ for $x>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dx} &= 120x-\dfrac{2800}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 120x &= \dfrac{2800}{x^2} \\ x^3 &= \dfrac{70}{3} \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{70}{3}}\approx2.858 \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}=120+\dfrac{5600}{x^3}>0 \text{ for } x>0$$
so the stationary point is a minimum.

The width is $x\approx2.858$ m, the length is $3x\approx8.573$ m, and the height is $h=\dfrac{10}{x^2}\approx1.225$ m.
$$\therefore\ \text{width } 2.858 \text{ m, length } 8.573 \text{ m, height } 1.225 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds $x\approx2.858$ and shows it is a minimum, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: blank x and y axes for sketching
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
Show that there are points of inflection at $x=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
What value does $y$ approach when $x\to\infty$ ?

Sketch $y=1-e^{-x^2}$, showing all asymptotes, turning points and points of inflection.

\exfigure{394_q33_1}

solutions.latex:
$$y=1-e^{-x^2}$$
Using the chain rule,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xe^{-x^2}$$
Stationary points: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Since $e^{-x^2}>0$, this needs $2x=0$, so $x=0$ and $y=1-e^{0}=0$.

For the nature, use the second derivative (product rule with $u=2x$, $v=e^{-x^2}$):
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2e^{-x^2}-4x^2e^{-x^2}=e^{-x^2}\left(2-4x^2\right)$$
At $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2>0$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and the stationary point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a),
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-x^2}\left(2-4x^2\right)$$
Possible inflections: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$. Since $e^{-x^2}>0$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2-4x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ x &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Test for a change in concavity (the sign of $2-4x^2$ decides the sign):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &< 0 &&\text{for } x<-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &&\text{concave down}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &> 0 &&\text{for } -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<x<\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &&\text{concave up}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &< 0 &&\text{for } x>\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at both values, so there are points of inflection at $x=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

meta.self_check: sign of 2-4x^2 on each interval checked.

solutions.latex:
As $x\to\infty$, $x^2\to\infty$, so $e^{-x^2}\to0$.
$$\therefore\ y\to1-0=1$$

Features: the minimum at $(0,0)$ (part (a)), the points of inflection at $x=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ where
$$y=1-e^{-\frac{1}{2}}\approx0.39$$
and the horizontal asymptote $y=1$ from part (c). The function is even, so the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis, with the same asymptote as $x\to-\infty$.

\exfigure{394_q33_s1}
criteria: Draws a graph with any two of the three features (asymptote, turning point, points of inflection) correct, or equivalent merit

Dot at minimum (0,0); dots at the inflection points (+-1/sqrt2, 1-e^{-1/2}), labelled in exact form with stacked fractions (rule 23); the approximation (+-0.71, 0.39) is left to the solution text. Asymptote y=1 dashed (aux) and labelled. Round 2 stretched y so the inflection labels sit clear of the x-axis.

1923.stem:
A circular Ferris wheel rotates at a constant rate, and the height of a certain passenger above the ground as a function of time can be modelled by the equation:

$$h(t)=20\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right)+22,$$

where $h(t)$ represents the height in metres and t is the time in seconds.

parts.latex: What is the maximum height of the person during the ride?
Show that the Ferris wheel completes 15 full rotations during a 10-minute ride.
A passenger can view the harbour from any height above 30m. After the Ferris wheel starts the ride, when will the passenger reach height of 30m for the first time?
How long will the passenger stay above 30m during the 10-minute ride? Answer in minutes and seconds.

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is $20$ and the centre line is $y=22$, so
$$h_{\max}=22+20=42 \text{ m}$$

For $h(t)=20\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right)+22$ the period is
$$T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{20}}=40 \text{ seconds}$$
A 10-minute ride lasts $10\times60=600$ seconds, so the number of rotations is
$$\dfrac{600}{40}=15$$
criteria: Finds the period $40$ seconds, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Solve $h(t)=30$ for the first $t\ge0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 20\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right)+22 &= 30 \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right) &= \dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$$
Let $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)$. At $t=0$, $\theta=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, and $\theta$ increases with $t$. On $-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ the first solution of $\sin\theta=0.4$ is $\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.4)\approx0.4115$ (the other solutions below this lie before the ride starts).
$$\begin{aligned} t-15 &= \dfrac{20}{\pi}\times0.4115 \\ t &\approx15+2.62 \\ &\approx17.6 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

meta.self_check: python: t=17.6198; h(0)=7.86 so no earlier crossing.

solutions.latex:
In each cycle the passenger is above $30$ m when $\sin\theta>0.4$, that is for
$$\sin^{-1}(0.4)<\theta<\pi-\sin^{-1}(0.4)$$
This is an angle of $\pi-2\sin^{-1}(0.4)\approx2.318$, and $\theta$ changes by $\dfrac{\pi}{20}$ per second, so the time above $30$ m in one cycle is
$$\dfrac{2.318}{\frac{\pi}{20}}\approx14.76 \text{ seconds}$$
There are $15$ full cycles in the ride (part (b)).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{time} &\approx15\times14.76 \\ &\approx221.4 \text{ seconds} \\ &\approx3 \text{ minutes } 41 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the time above $30$ m in one cycle, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: python: numeric count of h>30 over 0..600 s = 221.4 s.

parts.latex:
A substance decomposes at a rate that is proportional to the mass of the substance remaining. The remaining mass (M) can be modelled using the formula $M=M_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is the time in hours, $M_0$ is the initial mass and $k$ is a constant.

Initially there is 30 kg of the substance. After 24 hours half of the substance has decomposed.

Determine how long it will take for 90% of the substance to decompose.

solutions.latex:
Half decomposes after $24$ hours, so $M=15$ when $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} 15 &= 30e^{-24k} \\ e^{-24k} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln2}{24} \end{aligned}$$
$90\%$ decomposed leaves $10\%$, so $M=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 30e^{-kt} \\ e^{-kt} &= \dfrac{1}{10} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln10}{k} \\ &= \dfrac{24\ln10}{\ln2} \\ &\approx79.7 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $e^{-kt}=\dfrac{1}{10}$ with the correct $k$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $M=15$ and $t=24$ into the formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is $\int x^2(2x^3+1)^5\,dx$ ?

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x^3+1\right)=6x^2$, write $x^2=\dfrac{1}{6}\times 6x^2$ and use the rule:
$$\int f'(x)\big[f(x)\big]^n\,dx=\dfrac{\big[f(x)\big]^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int x^2(2x^3+1)^5\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{6}\int 6x^2(2x^3+1)^5\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{(2x^3+1)^6}{6}+C \\ &=\dfrac{(2x^3+1)^6}{36}+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $\ln(x+2)+\sqrt{9-x}$ ?

solutions.latex:
$\ln(x+2)$ needs $x+2>0$, so $x>-2$.

$\sqrt{9-x}$ needs $9-x\ge 0$, so $x\le 9$.
$$\therefore\ \text{domain } (-2,9]$$

parts.latex: Find $\int (e+\sin 2x)\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
$e$ is a constant, so $\displaystyle\int e\,dx=ex$, and $\displaystyle\int\sin ax\,dx=-\dfrac{\cos ax}{a}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int(e+\sin 2x)\,dx&=ex-\dfrac{\cos 2x}{2}+c\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_7 4x$ ?

solutions.latex:
Change of base: $\log_7 4x=\dfrac{\ln 4x}{\ln 7}$, and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln 4x}{\ln 7}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{\ln 7}\times\dfrac{4}{4x} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{x\ln 7}\end{aligned}$$

options.label: A
options.latex: A geometric series with common ratio of $-3$.

options.label: B
options.latex: A geometric series with common ratio of $-\log_a 3$.

options.label: C
options.latex: An arithmetic series with common difference $-3$

options.label: D
options.latex: An arithmetic series with common difference of $-\log_a 3$.

parts.latex:
Consider the series $\log_a 54+\log_a 18+\log_a 6+\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots$

Which of the following statements best describe the series?

solutions.latex:
Find the differences between consecutive terms:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_a 18-\log_a 54&=\log_a\dfrac{18}{54}=\log_a 3^{-1}=-\log_a 3 \\ \log_a 6-\log_a 18&=\log_a\dfrac{6}{18}=\log_a 3^{-1}=-\log_a 3\end{aligned}$$
The differences are constant, so the series is arithmetic with common difference $-\log_a 3$.

parts.latex:
Bella recently did a Maths test and an English test. The class scores on each test were normally distributed. The mean on the English test was 60%, and the standard deviation was 10%. Bella’s mark was 72%.

The mean on the Maths test was 73%, and the standard deviation was 5%.

What was Bella’s mark in the Maths test, if her $z$-scores in English and Maths were equal?

solutions.latex:
The $z$-score is $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$. English: $\mu=60$, $\sigma=10$, $x=72$:
$$z=\dfrac{72-60}{10}=1.2$$
Maths has the same $z$-score, with $\mu=73$ and $\sigma=5$:
$$\begin{aligned}M&=\mu+z\sigma \\ &=73+1.2\times 5 \\ &=79\%\end{aligned}$$

1931.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=f(x)$, which is made of two-line segments, a semi-circle and two quarters of a circle.

\exfigure{402_q7_1}

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) on a grid: two line segments, a semicircle and two quarter circles, x from 0 to 10

parts.latex: Which of the following is the value of $\int_0^{10} f(x)\,dx$ ?

solutions.latex:
Split the area into pieces, using the grid:

From $x=0$ to $x=2$ the area is a trapezium with parallel sides $2$ and $1$ and height $2$: $\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times(2+1)=3$.

From $x=2$ to $x=6$ the area is a rectangle $4\times 2=8$ with a semicircle of radius $2$ on top: $\dfrac{1}{2}\times\pi\times 2^2=2\pi$.

From $x=6$ to $x=8$ the quarter circle of radius $2$ is above the axis (area $\pi$), and from $x=8$ to $x=10$ the quarter circle of radius $2$ is below the axis (area $-\pi$), so they cancel.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{10}f(x)\,dx&=3+(8+2\pi)+(\pi-\pi) \\ &=11+2\pi\end{aligned}$$

402_q7_1.notes: Rules 1,3,4,6,9,12,13,19: purple Desmos curve drawn black 0.9pt; pieces computed exactly (segments (0,0)-(1,2)-(2,2), semicircle centre (4,2) r 2, quarter circles centres (6,0) and (10,0)) and joined. Paper's unequal axis scales kept (58.7 vs 55.1 px per unit), so the circles are very slightly elliptical exactly as on the paper. Light grey grid (minor 0.5, major 2) as on the paper; tick numbers sit on grid lines as in the original.

parts.latex: Let $h(x)=f(g(x))$, with $f(4)=1$, $f'(4)=6$, $g(2)=4$ and $g'(2)=4$. What is the equation of the tangent to the graph of $y=h(x)$ at $x=2$?

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule, $h'(x)=f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}h'(2)&=f'(g(2))\cdot g'(2) \\ &=f'(4)\times 4 \\ &=6\times 4 \\ &=24\end{aligned}$$
Also $h(2)=f(g(2))=f(4)=1$, so the tangent passes through $(2,1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-1&=24(x-2) \\ y&=24x-48+1 \\ &=24x-47\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Simplify $\cot\left(270^\circ+x^\circ\right)\cos\left(-x^\circ\right)+\cos\left(90^\circ+x^\circ\right)$

solutions.latex:
Reduce each term using the angle relationships:
$$\begin{aligned}\cot(270^\circ+x)&=\cot\big(360^\circ-(90^\circ-x)\big)=-\cot(90^\circ-x)=-\tan x \\ \cos(-x)&=\cos x \\ \cos(90^\circ+x)&=\cos\big(180^\circ-(90^\circ-x)\big)=-\cos(90^\circ-x)=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}-\tan x\cos x-\sin x&=-\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\times\cos x-\sin x \\ &=-\sin x-\sin x \\ &=-2\sin x\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the probability of rolling 3?

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$, and from the table $P(3)=3^k$ and $P(4)=3^{2k+1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{7}{16}+\dfrac{5}{16}+3^k+3^{2k+1}&=1 \\ 3^k+3^{2k+1}&=\dfrac{1}{4} \\ 4\left(3^k\right)+4\left(3^{2k}\cdot 3\right)-1&=0\end{aligned}$$
Let $m=3^k$, so $3^{2k}=m^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}12m^2+4m-1&=0 \\ (2m+1)(6m-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$m=3^k>0$, so $m\ne-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $m=\dfrac{1}{6}$.
$$\therefore\ P(3)=3^k=\dfrac{1}{6}$$

1936.stem:
The following table shows the probability distribution of a discrete random variable with an expected value of two.

\extable{402_q12_t1}

parts.latex: Calculate the values of $a$ and $b$.
Hence calculate the standard deviation, correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}0.2+0.1+a+b+0.2&=1 \\ a+b&=0.5 &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
The expected value is $2$:
$$\begin{aligned}0\times 0.2+1\times 0.1+2a+3b+4\times 0.2&=2 \\ 0.1+2a+3b+0.8&=2 \\ 2a+3b&=1.1 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Substitute $a=0.5-b$ from (1) into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}2(0.5-b)+3b&=1.1 \\ 1+b&=1.1 \\ b&=0.1\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that the curve $y=3x^2-5\ln x$ is concave up for all values of $x>0$.

solutions.latex:
Concave up means $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=6x-\dfrac{5}{x} \\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=6+\dfrac{5}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
For $x>0$, $x^2>0$, so $\dfrac{5}{x^2}>0$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6+\dfrac{5}{x^2}>0$.

$\therefore$ the curve is concave up for all $x>0$.
criteria: Finds the second derivative but fails to justify the concavity

parts.latex: Differentiate $e^{4x}\ln(x^2)$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\ln\left(x^2\right)=2\ln x$, the function is $2e^{4x}\ln x$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{4x} & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=4e^{4x} & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2e^{4x}\ln x\right)&=2\left(4e^{4x}\ln x+e^{4x}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\\ &=8e^{4x}\ln x+\dfrac{2e^{4x}}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=8e^{4x}\ln x+\dfrac{2e^{4x}}{x}=2e^{4x}\left(4\ln x+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$$
criteria: Partially correct use of the product rule

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly uses the product rule and writes the derivative in the form $u'v+v'u$

parts.latex: Show that the angle HPB is $110^\circ$.
Find the distance BH correct to three decimal places.
Find the bearing of Kate’s house H from the beach B.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{402_q16_s1}

Draw a north line at $H$ and at $P$; they are parallel. The bearing of $P$ from $H$ is $320^\circ$, so the angle between $HP$ and north at $H$ is $360^\circ-320^\circ=40^\circ$.

Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to $180^\circ$ (with $N$ due north of $P$):
$$\angle NPH=180^\circ-40^\circ=140^\circ$$
The bearing of $B$ from $P$ is $250^\circ$, measured clockwise from the north line at $P$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\angle HPB&=250^\circ-140^\circ\\ &=110^\circ\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Shows clearly why $\angle HPB$ is $110^\circ$ by marking the alternate/co-interior angles subtended by the compass directions on the diagram

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{402_q16_s3}

In $\triangle HPB$, $HP=4$, $PB=5$ and $\angle HPB=110^\circ$ (part (i)), so use the cosine rule for the side opposite the given angle.
$$\begin{aligned}BH^2&=5^2+4^2-2.5.4\cos110^\circ\\ &=41-40\cos110^\circ\\ &\approx54.681\\ BH&=\sqrt{41-40\cos110^\circ}\\ &\approx7.395\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BH\approx7.395\text{ km}$$
criteria: Uses the cosine rule but fails to obtain the correct value of $BH$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: answer was 7.39 km (2 d.p.); the question asks for 3 d.p., so it is now 7.395 km ($\sqrt{54.6808}=7.3946$).
meta.top_criterion_original: Successfully uses the cosine rule to find the correct distance of $BH$

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{402_q16_s2}

In $\triangle HPB$ the side $HP=4$ is opposite $\angle HBP$, and $BH\approx7.395$ is opposite the $110^\circ$ angle (part (b)). Use the sine rule:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle HBP}{4}=\dfrac{\sin110^\circ}{7.395}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle HBP&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4\sin110^\circ}{7.395}\right)\\ &\approx30.6^\circ\end{aligned}$$
($\angle HBP$ is acute because $\angle HPB$ is already obtuse.)

The bearing of $P$ from $B$ is $250^\circ-180^\circ=70^\circ$, and $H$ lies a further $\angle HBP$ clockwise from $BP$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{bearing of }H\text{ from }B&=70^\circ+30.6^\circ\\ &\approx101^\circ\text{T}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows elements of successful working towards the solution

parts.latex: If $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, solve $\sqrt{2}\cos\left(2\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-1=0$.

solutions.latex:
Isolate the cosine:
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}\cos\left(2\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=1\\ \cos\left(2\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Adjust the domain, one operation per line:
$$\begin{aligned}0&\le\theta\le2\pi\\ 0&\le2\theta\le4\pi &&(\text{multiply by }2)\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{3}&\le2\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\dfrac{11\pi}{3} &&(\text{subtract }\dfrac{\pi}{3})\end{aligned}$$
Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants and the acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so for $u=2\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$u=-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{9\pi}{4}$$
Add $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to each value, then divide by $2$:
$$2\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{25\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{31\pi}{12}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{24},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{24},\ \dfrac{25\pi}{24},\ \dfrac{31\pi}{24}$$
criteria: Finds correct values for $\theta$ but misses certain solutions, OR incorrectly simplifies the trig equation but finds all the correct solutions

meta.top_criterion_original: Finds all correct values for $\theta$ within the specified domain

parts.latex:
Explain why the geometric series shown below does not have a limiting sum.

$$3+\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}-1}+\dfrac{3}{\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)^2}+\ldots..$$

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is the second term divided by the first:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}-1}\div3\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}-1}\\ &\approx1.37\end{aligned}$$
A geometric series has a limiting sum only if $-1<r<1$. Since $r>1$, there is no limiting sum.
criteria: Only manages to correctly state the value of $r$

meta.top_criterion_original: States the value of the common ratio $r$ and correctly justifies why the series does not have a limiting sum

parts.latex:
The future value of an annuity when \$1 is invested at the start of each period is shown in the table below.

\extable{402_q19_t1}

Jamie deposits \$800 into a savings account at the start of each month for 6 months. After the 6th deposit, Jamie stops making deposits but leaves the money in the savings account until exactly 12 months from the first deposit.

The interest rate on her savings account is 12% per annum, compounded monthly. What is the balance of Jamie’s savings account at the end of the 12 months?
parts.note: Annuity future value interest-factor TABLE look-up: 2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only

solutions.latex:
The table gives the future value of $\$1$ invested at the start of each period. Here the rate is $\dfrac{12\%}{12}=1\%$ per month and there are $6$ deposits, so the table factor is $6.2135$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{FV after 6 months}&=800\times6.2135\\ &=\$4970.80\end{aligned}$$
No more deposits are made, so this amount earns compound interest for a further $6$ months at $1\%$ per month, using $A=P(1+r)^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Balance}&=4970.80\times1.01^6\\ &\approx\$5276.60\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the balance after 12 months is }\$5276.60$$
criteria: Finds the FV correctly but incorrectly finds the final balance, OR fails to find the FV properly but correctly finds the final balance using the compound interest formula (carry error)

parts.latex: Prove that $f(x)$ represents a probability density function.
State the mode of the distribution.
Explain why the median is equal to the mode in this distribution.
Find $P(X>1.5)$.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, $f(x)\ge0$ for all $x$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$.

For $0\le x\le2$, both $x\ge0$ and $2-x\ge0$, so $f(x)\ge0$; elsewhere $f(x)=0$. For the area:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx&=\int_0^2\dfrac{3}{4}\left(2x-x^2\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left[x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left(4-\dfrac{8}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot\dfrac{4}{3}\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(x)\ge0$ and the total area is $1$, $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Correctly integrates the function but fails at correctly arriving at $1$ upon substitution, OR shows elements of successful working towards the solution

meta.top_criterion_original: Shows via integration that $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$ and hence is a PDF

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=\dfrac{3x}{4}(2-x)$ is a concave down parabola with $x$-intercepts $0$ and $2$. The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest, on the axis of symmetry, halfway between the $x$-intercepts:
$$\text{mode}=\dfrac{0+2}{2}=1$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly justifies that the distribution is symmetrical about the mode and thus the mode must equal the median

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>1.5)&=\int_{1.5}^{2}\dfrac{3}{4}\left(2x-x^2\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left[x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{1.5}^{2}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left[\left(4-\dfrac{8}{3}\right)-\left(2.25-1.125\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}-\dfrac{9}{8}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot\dfrac{5}{24}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{32}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X>1.5)=\dfrac{5}{32}=0.15625$$
criteria: Writes the correct expression for the definite integral but fails at arriving at the correct answer, OR finds the complement of this event

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the antiderivative was written as $\frac{3}{4}(2x-x^2)$ (the integrand) and substituted to give a negative value; the antiderivative is $\frac{3}{4}\left(x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right)$. The answer $\frac{5}{32}$ is unchanged.
meta.top_criterion_original: Successfully integrates the function to find the probability

The diagram shows the graph of $y=a^x$, where $a>1$. Also shown on the diagram are 4 inner rectangles of width 1 unit.

figures.cap: graph of y=a^x with 4 inner rectangles of width 1 on x from 0 to 4, NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex: Show that the area of the 4 rectangles is $\dfrac{a^4-1}{a-1}\ u^2$.
By finding the area under the curve $y=a^x$ between $x=0$ and $x=4$, and using the result in part (i), prove that $\ln a<a-1$.

solutions.latex:
Each rectangle has width $1$, and its height is the value of the curve at the left end of its strip: $a^0,\ a^1,\ a^2,\ a^3$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=1.1+1\cdot a+1\cdot a^2+1\cdot a^3\\ &=1+a+a^2+a^3\end{aligned}$$
This is a geometric series with first term $1$, common ratio $a$ and $4$ terms, so $S_n=\dfrac{T_1\left(r^n-1\right)}{r-1}$ gives
$$A=\dfrac{1\cdot\left(a^4-1\right)}{a-1}=\dfrac{a^4-1}{a-1}\text{ u}^2$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 2 marks for the full solution (show how to get the area of each rectangle and state the G.P. with $r=a$, $a=1$)

solutions.latex:
The area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4a^x\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{a^4-1}{\ln a}\end{aligned}$$
The curve is increasing, so the inner rectangles lie under it and their area is less than the area under the curve:
$$\dfrac{a^4-1}{a-1}<\dfrac{a^4-1}{\ln a}$$
Since $a>1$, the quantities $a^4-1$, $a-1$ and $\ln a$ are all positive. Divide both sides by $a^4-1$, then take reciprocals of the positive sides, which reverses the inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{a-1}&<\dfrac{1}{\ln a}\\ a-1&>\ln a\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \ln a<a-1$$

1946.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}3^{-x}\ln 3 & \text{for } x\ge 0\\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.
Find the exact value of the third quartile.

solutions.latex:
For $x\ge0$ the cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^xf(t)\,dt$, and $F(x)=0$ for $x<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x3^{-t}\ln3\,dt\\ &=\left[-3^{-t}\right]_0^x\\ &=1-3^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}1-3^{-x} & \text{for }x\ge0\\ 0 & \text{for }x<0\end{cases}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 2 marks for the correct cumulative distribution function

solutions.latex:
The third quartile $Q_3$ satisfies $F(Q_3)=0.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-3^{-x}&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ 3^{-x}&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ -x\ln3&=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}=-\ln4\\ x&=\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ Q_3=\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln3}$$

parts.latex: Sketch the graph of the curve $y=\dfrac{5x^2e^{\frac{x}{2}}}{3}$ showing the coordinates of the turning points and their nature.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\dfrac{5x^2}{3} & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=\dfrac{10x}{3} & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{10x}{3}e^{\frac{x}{2}}+\dfrac{5x^2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{5x}{3}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(2+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$. Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}\ne0$, either $\dfrac{5x}{3}=0$ or $2+\dfrac{x}{2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=0, & y&=0\\ x&=-4, & y&=\dfrac{5.16}{3}e^{-2}=\dfrac{80}{3e^2}\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $y'$ either side of each point:
$$\begin{aligned}x=-5:&\quad y'\approx0.34>0\\ x=-4:&\quad y'=0\\ x=-1:&\quad y'\approx-1.5<0\end{aligned}$$
so $\left(-4,\dfrac{80}{3e^2}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.
$$\begin{aligned}x=-1:&\quad y'\approx-1.5<0\\ x=0:&\quad y'=0\\ x=1:&\quad y'\approx6.9>0\end{aligned}$$
so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.

As $x\to-\infty$, $y\to0^{+}$, so the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

parts.latex: Differentiate $\ln\left(3\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^3$.

solutions.latex:
By the log law $\ln A^n=n\ln A$:
$$\ln\left(3\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^3=3\ln\left(3\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$$
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ with $f(x)=3\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$ and $f'(x)=\dfrac{3}{2}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3\cdot\dfrac{\frac{3}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}}{3\sin\frac{x}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}\cot\dfrac{x}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively (also accepted), differentiate $\ln u^3$ directly, where $u=3\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3\left(3\sin\frac{x}{2}\right)^2\cdot\frac{3}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}}{\left(3\sin\frac{x}{2}\right)^3}=\dfrac{3}{2}\cot\dfrac{x}{2}$$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}\int_0^3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}g(x)+3x\right)dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^3g(x)\,dx+\int_0^33x\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot11+\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}\right]_0^3\\ &=\dfrac{11}{2}+\dfrac{27}{2}\\ &=19\end{aligned}$$

A person from those who were surveyed last Sunday is to be selected at random. What is the probability that this person chose French or Italian but not Japanese?
Two people are chosen at random, what is the probability of both chose French only?

solutions.latex:
French or Italian but not Japanese: the regions $F$ only, $I$ only and $F\cap I$ only, so $9+7+8=24$ people.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{9+7+8}{45}\\ &=\dfrac{24}{45}\\ &=\dfrac{8}{15}\end{aligned}$$

Two people are chosen without replacement and $9$ of the $45$ chose French only:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{9}{45}\cdot\dfrac{8}{44}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{55}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\left(\cot\theta+\operatorname{cosec}\theta\right)^2=\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta}$.

solutions.latex:
Write $\cot\theta$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, then use $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2\\ &=\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta+1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{1-\cos^2\theta} &&\left(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{(1-\cos\theta)(1+\cos\theta)} &&(\text{difference of two squares})\\ &=\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta} &&(\text{cancel }1+\cos\theta)\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

1953.stem:
Consider the following diagram with the cone inscribed in a sphere.

\exfigure{402_q29_1}

figures.cap: cone ABC inscribed in a sphere with centre O, radius R, base radius r, height h
solution sketch: cone-in-sphere diagram with OA = R and OD = h - R marked

parts.latex: If $r$ is the radius of the cone show that $r^2=2hR-h^2$.
Show that the volume of the cone that can be inscribed in a sphere of radius $R$ is given by $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)$ where $h$ is the height of the inscribed cone.
Show that the volume of the largest cone is $\dfrac{8}{27}$ of the volume of the sphere.

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$. Substitute $r^2=2hR-h^2$ from part (i):
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2hR-h^2\right)h\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)\end{aligned}$$

Let $V_C=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)$ be the volume of the cone and $V_S=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3$ the volume of the sphere. Differentiate with respect to $h$:
$$\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4Rh-3h^2\right),\qquad\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4R-6h\right)$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4Rh-3h^2&=0\\ h\left(4R-3h\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$h=0$ is rejected since $h>0$, so $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$.

Second derivative test at $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(4R-6\cdot\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(4R-8R)\\ &=-\dfrac{4\pi R}{3}\end{aligned}$$
This is negative since $R>0$, so $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$ gives a maximum.

The maximum volume of the cone is
$$\begin{aligned}V_C&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(2R\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^2-\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^3\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{32R^3}{9}-\dfrac{64R^3}{27}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi\cdot\dfrac{96R^3-64R^3}{27}\\ &=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\end{aligned}$$
Compare with the sphere:
$$\dfrac{V_C}{V_S}=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\cdot\dfrac{3}{4\pi R^3}=\dfrac{8}{27}$$
Therefore the volume of the largest cone is $\dfrac{8}{27}$ of the volume of the sphere.

1954.stem:
(The table on page 27 can be used for this question)

Madelyn is a long jumper training for the national age championships. To be able to compete at the national age championships her longest jump must be able to be beaten by less than 0.17% of the general population.

The distance jumped by the general population is normally distributed with a mean of 3.48 metres and standard deviation of 1.08 metres.

\extable{402_q30_t1}

parts.latex: What is the minimum distance that Madelyn needs to jump, correct to the nearest centimetre?

solutions.latex:
Madelyn's jump $D$ must be beaten by less than $0.17\%$ of the population, so $P(X>D)<0.0017$. Standardise with $z=\dfrac{D-3.48}{1.08}$:
$$P(Z<z)>1-0.0017=0.9983$$
From the table, $P(Z\le2.93)=0.9983$, so $z=2.93$.
$$\begin{aligned}D&=\mu+z\sigma\\ &=3.48+2.93\times1.08\\ &=6.6444\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is }6.64\text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct $z$ score, or finds the distance correctly using an incorrect $z$ score

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct distance (1 mark for using an incorrect $z$ score to find the distance correctly)

figures.cap: parabola y^2=2x+6 and line y=x-1 with the enclosed region shaded, vertical lines at x=-1 and x=5

parts.latex: Determine the area of the region enclosed by $y^2=2x+6$ and $y=x-1$.
can_use: Area with respect to the y-axis

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $(x-1)^2=2x+6$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-2x+1&=2x+6\\ x^2-4x-5&=0\\ (x-5)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=-1$ or $x=5$, giving the points $(-1,-2)$ and $(5,4)$.

Method 1 (integrate with respect to $x$). From $x=-3$ to $x=-1$ the region lies between $y=-\sqrt{2x+6}$ and $y=\sqrt{2x+6}$. From $x=-1$ to $x=5$ it lies between the line and $y=\sqrt{2x+6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=2\int_{-3}^{-1}(2x+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}dx+\int_{-1}^{5}\left((2x+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}-x+1\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(2x+6)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{-3}^{-1}+\left[\dfrac{1}{3}(2x+6)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{2}{3}(0)\right]+\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{3}(16)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{25}{2}+5\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}(4)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}-1\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{16}{3}+\dfrac{38}{3}\\ &=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (integrate with respect to $y$). The line is $x=y+1$ and the parabola is $x=\dfrac{y^2}{2}-3$; between $y=-2$ and $y=4$ the line is to the right of the parabola.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_{-2}^{4}\left((y+1)-\left(\dfrac{y^2}{2}-3\right)\right)dy\\ &=\int_{-2}^{4}\left(y-\dfrac{y^2}{2}+4\right)dy\\ &=\left[\dfrac{y^2}{2}-\dfrac{y^3}{6}+4y\right]_{-2}^{4}\\ &=\left(8-\dfrac{32}{3}+16\right)-\left(2+\dfrac{4}{3}-8\right)\\ &=\dfrac{40}{3}+\dfrac{14}{3}\\ &=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is }18\text{ units}^2$$
