1956.stem: Madison is learning to drive. Her first lesson is 10 minutes long. Her second lesson is 15 minutes long. Each subsequent lesson is 5 minutes longer than the previous lesson.

parts.latex: How long will Madison's fifteenth lesson be?
How many hours of lessons will Madison have completed after her fifteenth lesson?
During which lesson will Madison have completed a total of 40 hours of driving lessons?

solutions.latex:
The lesson lengths $10+15+20+25+\ldots$ form an arithmetic series with first term $a=10$ and common difference $d=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_{15}&=a+(15-1)d\\ &=10+14\times5\\ &=80\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$

Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$, with $a=10$, $d=5$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{15}&=\dfrac{15}{2}\left[2(10)+(15-1)\cdot5\right]\\ &=\dfrac{15}{2}\cdot90\\ &=675\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$
Convert to hours: $675\div60=11.25$.
$$\therefore\ 11.25\text{ hours}=11\text{ hours }15\text{ minutes}$$

$40$ hours $=40\times60=2400$ minutes. Find $n$ with $S_n=2400$:
$$\begin{aligned}2400&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(10)+(n-1)\cdot5\right]\\ 4800&=n(15+5n)\\ 5n^2+15n-4800&=0\\ n^2+3n-960&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}n&=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{3^2-4(1)(-960)}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{3849}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=\dfrac{-3+\sqrt{3849}}{2}\approx29.5$.

Check with whole lessons: $S_{29}=2320<2400$ and $S_{30}=2475>2400$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Madison completes 40 hours during her 30th lesson}$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_2\left(2-2x\right)=\log_{\sqrt{2}}\left(1-x\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms need $1-x>0$, so $x<1$.

Method 1 (change of base to $\ln$). Using $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$ and $\ln\sqrt{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\ln(2-2x)}{\ln2}&=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\ln\sqrt{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\frac{1}{2}\ln2}\\ &=\dfrac{2\ln(1-x)}{\ln2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\ln(2-2x)&=2\ln(1-x)\\ 2-2x&=(1-x)^2\\ 2-2x&=1-2x+x^2\\ x^2&=1\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
Since $x<1$, $x=1$ is rejected. Check $x=-1$: $\log_2 4=2$ and $\log_{\sqrt{2}}2=2$.
$$\therefore\ x=-1$$
Method 2. Let $y$ be the common value, so $2-2x=2^y$, that is $1-x=2^{y-1}$, and $1-x=\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^y=2^{\frac{y}{2}}$. Equating the two expressions for $1-x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2^{y-1}&=2^{\frac{1}{2}y}\\ y-1&=\dfrac{1}{2}y\\ y&=2\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $1-x=2^{y-1}$ gives $1-x=2$, so $x=-1$.

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\left(\sin^3 2x^\circ\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Convert degrees to radians: $\pi$ radians $=180^\circ$, so $1^\circ=\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ and $2x^\circ=\dfrac{2\pi x}{180}=\dfrac{\pi x}{90}$ radians.
$$y=\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\right)^3$$
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\right)^2\cdot\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{90}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{30}\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\right)^2\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{90}\end{aligned}$$

1959.stem: Marge borrows \$50 000 in order to buy a car. The loan attracts an interest of just 0.5% per month. The company also offers an interest free period for the first six months. However, the first payment is due at the end of the first month. Marge agrees to repay the loan over 10 years, by making 120 equal monthly repayments of \$$M$. Let $A_n$ be the amount owing at the end of $n$th repayment, then

parts.latex: Show that $A_6=50\,000-6M$
Hence derive the expression for $A_{120}$ in simplest form.
Find the value of the monthly repayment to the nearest cent.

solutions.latex:
During the interest-free period each repayment of $M$ simply reduces the amount owing:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=50\,000-M\\ A_2&=A_1-M=50\,000-2M\\ A_3&=A_2-M=50\,000-3M\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_6&=50\,000-6M\end{aligned}$$

After the interest-free period, $0.5\%$ interest is added each month, so the balance is multiplied by $1.005$ before each repayment of $M$ is taken off:
$$\begin{aligned}A_7&=A_6\times1.005-M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005-M\\ A_8&=A_7\times1.005-M\\ &=\left[(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005-M\right]\cdot1.005-M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005^2-M\cdot1.005-M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)\cdot1.005^2-M(1.005+1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for $A_7$ in terms of $M$ only

solutions.latex:
Each month the balance is multiplied by $1.005$ and $M$ is subtracted, so the pattern of part (ii) continues up to $A_{120}$, with $114$ months of interest after $A_6$. The terms multiplying $M$ form a geometric series with first term $1$, common ratio $1.005$ and $114$ terms, so $S_n=\dfrac{r^n-1}{r-1}$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}A_{120}&=(50\,000-6M)(1.005)^{114}-\left(1.005^{113}+1.005^{112}+\cdots+1.005+1\right)M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)(1.005)^{114}-\dfrac{1.005^{114}-1}{1.005-1}M\\ &=(50\,000-6M)(1.005)^{114}-200\left(1.005^{114}-1\right)M\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds expression for $A_{120}$ in terms of $M$ only
Sets $A_{120}=0$ and attempts to solve for $M$

1960.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. It’s displacement, $x$ metres, from the origin, $O$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t\ge0$, is given by $x=4+3te^{-2t}$

parts.latex: Show the velocity of the particle is given by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3e^{-2t}\left(1-2t\right)$.
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Find the greatest possible total distance the particle could travel.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of the constant $4$ is $0$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(3te^{-2t}\right)$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3t & v&=e^{-2t}\\ u'&=3 & v'&=-2e^{-2t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=3e^{-2t}+3t\cdot\left(-2e^{-2t}\right)\\ &=3e^{-2t}-6te^{-2t}\\ &=3e^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to differentiate using the product rule

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$. At $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=3e^{-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}\left(1-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=3e^{-1}(1-1)\\ &=0\end{aligned}$$
Hence the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The particle starts at $x=4$. Since $3e^{-2t}\ne0$, $v=0$ only when $1-2t=0$, that is at $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving right}\\ v&<0 &&\text{for }t>\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
At the turning point:
$$x=4+3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-1}=4+\dfrac{3}{2e}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $x=4+\dfrac{3t}{e^{2t}}\to4+0=4$, approached from above but never reached.

Distance travelled moving right: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.

Distance travelled moving left, back towards $x=4$: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{greatest total distance}=\dfrac{3}{2e}+\dfrac{3}{2e}=\dfrac{3}{e}\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Calculates distance travelled in first half of journey, namely $\dfrac{3}{2e}$ metres

parts.latex:
Sally contributes \$7200 each year into a superannuation fund for the first 15 years of her working life. For the next 20 years until retirement, she decides to increase this, and invest a total of \$10000 each year. Each contribution is paid at the beginning of the year.

If the investment earns 7% per annum paid yearly over whole period, how much will her investment be upon retiring? (Show all your working)

solutions.latex:
Each contribution is paid at the start of the year, so the first contribution earns interest for the whole $15$ years. After $15$ years the amount is a geometric series with first term $7200(1.07)$, common ratio $1.07$ and $15$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=7200(1.07)\\ A_2&=\left(A_1+7200\right)(1.07)=7200(1.07)^2+7200(1.07)\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_{15}&=7200(1.07)^{15}+7200(1.07)^{14}+\cdots+7200(1.07)^2+7200(1.07)\\ &=\dfrac{7200(1.07)\left(1.07^{15}-1\right)}{1.07-1}\\ &=193\,593.9855\ldots\end{aligned}$$
From then on the contributions are $\$10\,000$ at the start of each year. The new contributions form a geometric series with first term $10\,000(1.07)$, common ratio $1.07$ and $20$ terms, and $A_{15}$ grows for a further $20$ years:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{16}&=\left(A_{15}+10\,000\right)(1.07)=A_{15}(1.07)+10\,000(1.07)\\ A_{17}&=\left(A_{16}+10\,000\right)(1.07)=A_{15}(1.07)^2+10\,000(1.07)^2+10\,000(1.07)\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_{35}&=A_{15}(1.07)^{20}+10\,000(1.07)^{20}+10\,000(1.07)^{19}+\cdots+10\,000(1.07)\\ &=A_{15}(1.07)^{20}+\dfrac{10\,000(1.07)\left(1.07^{20}-1\right)}{1.07-1}\\ &\approx\$1\,187\,799.41\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{her investment on retiring is }\$1\,187\,799.41\text{ (nearest cent)}$$
criteria: Successively finds $A_{16}$ and $A_{17}$ or an expression for $A_{35}$ with working

parts.latex: What is the gradient of the line with equation $2x-3y+1=0$

solutions.latex:
Make $y$ the subject:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-3y+1 &= 0 \\ 3y &= 2x+1 \\ y &= \dfrac{2}{3}x+\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

The graph of a function $y=\dfrac{4}{x+1}$ is translated 3 units left, and dilated vertically by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Which of the following gives the equation of the new function?

solutions.latex:
Translating $3$ units left replaces $x$ with $x+3$:
$$y=\dfrac{4}{(x+3)+1}=\dfrac{4}{x+4}$$
A vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $y$ with $2y$ (that is, $y$ becomes half as large):
$$2y=\dfrac{4}{x+4}$$

parts.latex:
Three chess players are chosen from 3 males and 7 females.

What is the probability that they are all the same gender?

solutions.latex:
Choose $3$ from $10$ people: $\binom{10}{3}=120$ ways.

All male: $\binom{3}{3}=1$ way. All female: $\binom{7}{3}=35$ ways.
$$P=\dfrac{1+35}{120}=\dfrac{36}{120}=\dfrac{3}{10}$$

parts.latex:
What is the domain of the function:

$$y=-\sqrt{1+3x}$$

solutions.latex:
The square root needs a non-negative number under it:
$$\begin{aligned} 1+3x &\ge 0 \\ 3x &\ge -1 \\ x &\ge -\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So the domain is $\left[-\dfrac{1}{3},\infty\right)$. The endpoint is included, and infinity is never a bracketed endpoint.

parts.latex: What is the solution of $3^x=2$

solutions.latex:
Take natural logarithms of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(3^x\right) &= \ln2 \\ x\ln3 &= \ln2 \\ x &= \dfrac{\log_e2}{\log_e3} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
$\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{12}f(x)\,dx$ is the area of two trapezoids, with signs (the graph is linear on each piece).

From $x=-4$ to $x=2$ (below the axis, parallel sides $11$ and $2$, width $6$):
$$\int_{-4}^{2}f(x)\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{2}(11+2)\times6=-39$$
From $x=2$ to $x=12$ (above the axis, parallel sides $6$ and $k$, width $10$):
$$\int_{2}^{12}f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}(6+k)\times10=30+5k$$
The total is $0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -39+30+5k &= 0 \\ 5k &= 9 \\ k &= 1.8 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $(\tan x+\cot x-1)(\sin x+\cos x)=\dfrac{\sec x}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x}+\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\sec^2x}$

solutions.latex:
Expand the left side, using $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\tan x\sin x+\tan x\cos x+\cot x\sin x+\cot x\cos x-\sin x-\cos x\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\sin x+\cos x+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}-\sin x-\cos x\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Now the right side, using $\sec x=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\dfrac{\sec x}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x}+\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\sec^2x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}\\ &=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expands the left side correctly, or equivalent merit

$$\ln x=3\quad\text{or}\quad\ln x=-1$$

parts.latex: $y=\dfrac{2e}{3x^3}$
$f(x)=x^3\log_e 4x$
$y=\dfrac{-\ln x}{x}$

solutions.latex:
Write the function as a power of $x$ ($2e$ is a constant):
$$y=\dfrac{2e}{3}x^{-3}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2ex^{-4}=-\dfrac{2e}{x^4}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3 & v&=\ln4x\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=\dfrac{4}{4x}=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^2\ln4x+x^3\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=3x^2\ln4x+x^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the product rule with one of $u'$, $v'$ correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-\ln x & v&=x\\ u'&=-\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{x\left(-\frac{1}{x}\right)-(-\ln x)}{x^2}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the quotient rule with one of $u'$, $v'$ correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $u=\sin(2x+1)$, so $y=u^3$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3\sin^2(2x+1)\cdot2\cos(2x+1)\\ &=6\sin^2(2x+1)\cos(2x+1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts the chain rule, or equivalent merit

1982.stem:
The diagram shows a sketch of the curve $y=6x^2-x^3$. The curve cuts the x axis at $A$, has a local maximum at $B$, and a point of inflexion at $C$.

\exfigure{416_q21_1}

figures.cap: sketch of y=6x^2-x^3 with points A, B and C

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of $A$.
Find the coordinates of $B$.
Find the coordinates of $C$.

solutions.latex:
$A$ is where the curve meets the $x$-axis, so put $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=6x^2-x^3\\ 0&=x^2(6-x)\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ (the origin) or $x=6$. $A$ is the intercept to the right of the origin.
$$\therefore\ A=(6,0)$$

$B$ is a stationary point, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=12x-3x^2\\ 12x-3x^2&=0\\ 3x(4-x)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=4$. Test with $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12-6x$:
$$\begin{aligned}x=0:&\quad\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12>0 &&\text{minimum (the origin)}\\ x=4:&\quad\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-12<0 &&\text{maximum}\end{aligned}$$
$B$ is the local maximum, so $x=4$ and $y=6(4)^2-4^3=32$.
$$\therefore\ B=(4,32)$$

$C$ is a point of inflexion, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ there and the concavity changes:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=12-6x\\ 12-6x&=0\\ x&=2\end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$ for $x<2$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$ for $x>2$, so the concavity changes. When $x=2$, $y=6(2)^2-2^3=16$.
$$\therefore\ C=(2,16)$$

parts.latex: Find the area bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=2$ and $x=6$ using the Trapezoidal Rule with five function values. Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

Calculate the same area by evaluating $\displaystyle\int_2^6\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$.

Explain why the Trapezoidal Rule overestimates the area.

solutions.latex:
Five function values at $x=2,3,4,5,6$ means $4$ strips, each of width $h=\dfrac{6-2}{4}=1$. With $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(2)+f(6)+2\left[f(3)+f(4)+f(5)\right]\right\}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{6}+2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\right]\\ &\approx1.117\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct trapezoidal rule expression, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}\int_2^6\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx&=\Big[\ln x\Big]_2^6\\ &=\ln6-\ln2\\ &=\ln3\\ &\approx1.099\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

For $x>0$, $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ has $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{x^3}>0$, so the curve is concave up. Each trapezium's top edge is a chord, which lies above a concave up curve, so the Trapezoidal Rule overestimates the area (as $1.117>1.099$).

1986.stem:
A particle with velocity, $v\,ms^{-1}$ moves along a straight line from a fixed point $O$

$$v=-4\cos t$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

It is initially 1 metre to the right of the origin.

parts.latex: When, and where, does the particle first come to rest?

Show that the total distance travelled by the particle between $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is

$(8-2\sqrt{3})$ metres.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$; the first time after $t=0$ is the smallest positive solution:
$$\begin{aligned}-4\cos t&=0\\ \cos t&=0\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$
For the position, integrate the velocity and use $x=1$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int-4\cos t\,dt\\ &=-4\sin t+C\\ 1&=0+C\\ x&=-4\sin t+1\end{aligned}$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x=-4+1=-3$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first comes to rest at }t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s, at }x=-3\text{ (3 m to the left of the origin)}$$
criteria: Finds $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and an expression for $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$v=-4\cos t$ changes sign at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so find the distance in each part separately:
$$\begin{aligned}v&<0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&\text{moving left}\\ v&>0 &&\text{for }\dfrac{\pi}{2}<t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3} &&\text{moving right}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=-4\end{aligned}$$
The particle moves left, so the distance travelled in this part is $4$ m.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\\ &=-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right)\\ &=4-2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total distance}=4+\left(4-2\sqrt{3}\right)=\left(8-2\sqrt{3}\right)\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in one of the two intervals, or equivalent merit
Identifies that the direction changes at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of $y=3x^4-4x^3+2$ in the space provided showing all:

\begin{itemize}
\item turning points
\item points of inflexion
\item y-intercept
\end{itemize}

There is no need to find the x-intercept(s).

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=12x^3-12x^2,\qquad\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=36x^2-24x$$
For turning points, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}12x^3-12x^2&=0\\ 12x^2(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=1$.

At $x=1$: $y=3-4+2=1$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=36-24=12>0$, so $(1,1)$ is a minimum turning point.

At $x=0$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$, so the second derivative test fails and the concavity is tested below.

For points of inflexion, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}36x^2-24x&=0\\ 12x(3x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$. When $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $y=3\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^4-4\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3+2=\dfrac{38}{27}$.

Test the concavity either side of each value:

\extable{Ts2888_1}

The concavity changes at both values. At $x=0$ the gradient is also $0$, so $(0,2)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion, not a turning point. $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{38}{27}\right)$ is also a point of inflexion.

The $y$-intercept is $(0,2)$.

\exfigure{416_q26_s1}

1988.stem:
The queueing time, $X$ minutes, of a teacher waiting on the phone with Department of Education has a probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3}{32}x(k-x), & 0\le x\le k\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex: Show that $k=4$.
Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.
Find the mode of the probability density function.
Find the probability that the phone will be answered within the first minute.
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^k\dfrac{3}{32}x(k-x)\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{3}{32}\left[\dfrac{kx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^k&=1\\ \dfrac{3}{32}\left(\dfrac{k^3}{2}-\dfrac{k^3}{3}\right)&=1\\ \dfrac{3}{32}\cdot\dfrac{k^3}{6}&=1\\ k^3&=64\\ k&=4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral equal to $1$ and integrates, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le4$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x\dfrac{3}{32}t(4-t)\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{3}{32}\left[2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^x\\ &=\dfrac{3}{32}\left(2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{3x^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{32}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{for }x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac{3x^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{32} & \text{for }0\le x\le4\\[6pt] 1 & \text{for }x>4\end{cases}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral for $F(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=\dfrac{3}{32}x(4-x)$ is a concave down parabola with $x$-intercepts $0$ and $4$, so its maximum is on the axis of symmetry, halfway between them:
$$\text{mode}=\dfrac{0+4}{2}=2$$

The phone is answered within the first minute when $X<1$, so use the cumulative distribution function from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<1)&=F(1)\\ &=\dfrac{3}{16}-\dfrac{1}{32}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{32}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Calculate the distance of the yacht from Island $B$ to the nearest kilometre.
Find the bearing of Island $B$ from the yacht to the nearest degree.

After spending several hours at the island, the speed boat travels due north back to Port $A$.

How far south of the port will the speed boat be when it is directly west of the yacht?

solutions.latex:
The yacht sails $3\times15=45$ km, so $AY=45$ km. Also $AB=30$ km, and the bearing $120^\circ$ is $60^\circ$ from due south, so $\angle YAB=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$. Use the cosine rule in $\triangle ABY$:
$$\begin{aligned}YB^2&=30^2+45^2-2\times30\times45\cos60^\circ\\ &=900+2025-1350\\ &=1575\\ YB&\approx39.7\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ YB\approx40\text{ km}$$
criteria: Uses the cosine rule with the correct sides and angle, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Needs drawn solution: a labelled triangle $ABY$ ($AB=30$, $AY=45$, $60^\circ$ at $A$, north line) at the top.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{416_q28_s1}

Use the sine rule in $\triangle ABY$, with the unrounded $YB=\sqrt{1575}\approx39.69$ km:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle YBA}{45}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{39.69}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle YBA&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{45\sin60^\circ}{39.69}\right)\\ &\approx79.1^\circ\end{aligned}$$
($\angle YBA$ is acute: by the cosine rule, $\cos\angle YBA=\dfrac{30^2+39.69^2-45^2}{2\times30\times39.69}\approx0.19>0$.)

The north-south lines through $A$, $B$ and $Y$ are parallel, so by alternate angles the angle between $YB$ and due south at $Y$ is $\angle YBA=79.1^\circ$. $B$ lies west of south from $Y$:
$$\text{bearing of }B\text{ from }Y=180^\circ+79.1^\circ\approx259^\circ\text{T}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: $YB\approx40$ was substituted into the sine rule, which gives $77^\circ$, but the answer $79^\circ$ comes from the unrounded $YB=39.69$; now worked with $39.69$. The bearing $259^\circ$T is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
The boat is directly west of the yacht when it is level with it, so its distance south of $A$ equals the yacht's distance south of $A$. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $AY=45$ km and $60^\circ$ at $A$, let $x$ be the southward distance, the side adjacent to the $60^\circ$ angle:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos60^\circ&=\dfrac{x}{45}\\ x&=22.5\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the speed boat is }22.5\text{ km south of the port}$$

parts.latex:
A small group of students were surveyed to determine whether they were part of the local baseball or tennis team.

\begin{itemize}
\item 16 people played tennis only.
\item 20 people played basketball only.
\item 5 people played neither.
\item $k$ people played both.
\end{itemize}

Let B be the event that a person plays baseball and let $T$ be the event that a person plays tennis.

Determine the value of $k$ such that the events B and $T$ are independent.

solutions.latex:
The total number of people is $16+20+5+k=41+k$. $B$ and $T$ are independent when $P(B\mid T)=P(B)$. Here $T$ has $16+k$ people and $B$ has $20+k$ people:
$$\dfrac{k}{16+k}=\dfrac{20+k}{41+k}$$
$$\begin{aligned}k(41+k)&=(16+k)(20+k)\\ 41k+k^2&=320+36k+k^2\\ 5k&=320\\ k&=64\end{aligned}$$
Check: $P(B\cap T)=\dfrac{64}{105}$ and $P(B)P(T)=\dfrac{84}{105}\cdot\dfrac{80}{105}=\dfrac{64}{105}$.
$$\therefore\ k=64$$
criteria: Sets up $P(B\mid T)=P(B)$ with correct expressions, or equivalent merit
States the condition for independence, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use the Empirical rule to determine the probability that the weight of one packet of coffee beans is less than the advertised weight of 300g.
In a shipment of 40 boxes, each with 100 packets of coffee beans, how many packets would be expected to be underweight?

Manufacturers aim to ensure that the expected number of underweight packets in the shipment will be less than 20. The machine is adjusted to give a mean weight of 308g, with the standard deviation of 3g remaining the same. Will they meet their target? Justify your answer.

solutions.latex:
$300$ g is $\dfrac{306-300}{3}=2$ standard deviations below the mean. By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of packets lie within $2$ standard deviations of the mean, so $5\%$ lie outside, half of them below:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<300)&=\dfrac{0.05}{2}\\ &=0.025=2.5\%\end{aligned}$$

The shipment has $40\times100=4000$ packets, and $2.5\%$ of them are expected to be underweight:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{expected number}&=0.025\times4000\\ &=100\text{ packets}\end{aligned}$$

With mean $308$ g, the $z$-score of $300$ g is
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{300-308}{3}\\ &\approx-2.67\end{aligned}$$
From the table:
$$\begin{aligned}P(Z<-2.67)&=1-P(Z\le2.67)\\ &=1-0.9962\\ &=0.0038\end{aligned}$$
$$0.0038\times4000=15.2\text{ packets}$$
Since $15.2<20$, they meet their target.
criteria: Finds the probability that a packet is underweight, or equivalent merit

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: $z$ was written as $-2.6$ ($-\frac{8}{3}=-2.67$) and the table value $0.996$ was used, giving $0.004$ and $16$ packets; now $z=-2.67$, $P=0.0038$, $15.2$ packets. The conclusion (target met) is unchanged.

1992.stem:
A prototype rocket which is initially at rest, takes off from a launchpad on the ground. It has a time of flight of $T$ seconds, and $t$ is the time in seconds, where $0\le t\le T$.

The velocity of the rocket, $v\,ms^{-1}$, is given by:

$$v(t)=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$

parts.latex:
Shortly after the rocket takes off, the engine stops and it begins to descend towards the ground.

Find the time at which the rocket begins to descend.
Before the rocket starts to descend it reaches its maximum velocity. Find the time it takes for the rocket to achieve its maximum velocity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The rocket rises while $v>0$ and begins to descend when $v$ returns to $0$ after take-off:
$$0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi,\ \ldots$$
$t=0$ is the take-off, and for $0<t<10$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)>0$ so $v>0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket begins to descend at }t=10\text{ s}$$
criteria: Sets $v=0$ and finds $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For maximum velocity, $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=0$. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=0.5e^t & v&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ u'&=0.5e^t & v'&=\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dv}{dt}&=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+0.5e^t\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ &=0.5e^t\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\right)\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=0\\ \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}\end{aligned}$$
The rocket is rising for $0<t<10$, so $0<\dfrac{\pi t}{10}<\pi$. Tangent is negative in the second quadrant, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=\pi-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)\approx2.837$$
$$t\approx2.837\cdot\dfrac{10}{\pi}\approx9.03\text{ s}$$
$v=0$ at $t=0$ and at $t=10$ and $v>0$ between them, so this stationary point is the maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket reaches its maximum velocity after }9.03\text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Differentiates and forms $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}$, or equivalent merit
Differentiates using the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: How many solutions does the equation $(\cos x-1)(2\sin x+1)=0$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$ have?

solutions.latex:
A product is zero when one of its factors is zero.

$\cos x-1=0$ gives $\cos x=1$, so $x=0$ or $x=2\pi$ (2 solutions).

$2\sin x+1=0$ gives $\sin x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$. The acute angle is $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$x=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
(2 solutions). The four values are different, so the equation has $4$ solutions.

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: acute angle was given as $\frac{\pi}{3}$ with solutions $\pi\pm\frac{\pi}{3}$ (those have $\sin x=\mp\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$); for $\sin x=-\frac{1}{2}$ the acute angle is $\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{11\pi}{6}$. The count of $4$ is unchanged.

parts.latex: $y=e^{2x}\cos 5x$
$g(x)=\sqrt{\ln 7+e^{x}}$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $u=\sin2x$, so $y=u^3$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3\sin^2(2x)\cdot2\cos2x\\ &=6\sin^22x\cos2x\end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=\cos5x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=-5\sin5x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2e^{2x}\cos5x+e^{2x}(-5\sin5x)\\ &=e^{2x}(2\cos5x-5\sin5x)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows attempt at product rule, gets $u'$ OR $v'$ correct

meta.marker_note: Also accept the non-factorised form $-5e^{2x}\sin5x+2e^{2x}\cos5x$.

solutions.latex:
Write $g(x)=\left(\ln7+e^x\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The term $\ln7$ is a constant. Using the chain rule, with inner function $\ln7+e^x$ whose derivative is $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}g'(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln7+e^x\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot e^x\\ &=\dfrac{e^x}{2\sqrt{\ln7+e^x}}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows attempt at differentiation using chain rule

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the chain-rule factor $e^x$ (derivative of $\ln7+e^x$) was missing, giving $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\ln7+e^x}}$; now $g'(x)=\dfrac{e^x}{2\sqrt{\ln7+e^x}}$ (checked numerically).
meta.marker_note: Allow $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln7+e^x\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^x$.

parts.latex:
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\cos(2x)$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Leave your answer in the form $y=mx+b$.

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2\sin2x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\ &=-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$y=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The tangent through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ with gradient $-\sqrt{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-\dfrac{1}{2}&=-\sqrt{3}\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\\ y&=-\sqrt{3}\,x+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi}{6}+\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that $\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$
Hence show that if $y=\log_x 2$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{x(\ln x)^2}$

solutions.latex:
Use the change of base rule, $\log_ab=\dfrac{\log_cb}{\log_ca}$, with base $2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\log_x2\\ &=\dfrac{\log_22}{\log_2x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Shows change of base formula (essential step)
meta.marker_note: The change of base step is essential and must be shown.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $y=\log_x2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}$. Change the base to $e$ using $\log_2x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{\ln x}{\ln2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln2}{\ln x}\\ &=\ln2\cdot(\ln x)^{-1}\end{aligned}$$
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\ln2\cdot(-1)(\ln x)^{-2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=-\dfrac{\ln2}{x(\ln x)^2}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Needs to show chain rule correctly

parts.latex: Consider the function $f(x)=2-\ln x$
Show that $f(x)$ is decreasing at a decreasing rate for all values of $x>0$.
Sketch the graph of $y=2-\ln x$ showing all key features.
Determine the coordinates of all points of inflexion on the curve $y=x^5-5x^4+1$.

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=2-\ln x$ for $x>0$.
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{1}{x}$$
Since $\dfrac{1}{x}>0$ for $x>0$, $f'(x)<0$, so $f(x)$ is decreasing for all $x>0$.
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2}>0\text{ for all }x>0$$
So $f'(x)$ is increasing: the gradient is negative and rising towards $0$, so the decrease gets slower. Hence $f(x)$ is decreasing at a decreasing rate (the graph is concave up).
criteria: Attempts to differentiate and explains $f'(x)<0$ for all $x>0$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: $f''(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2}>0$ was labelled 'concave down'; it is concave up (this is what 'decreasing at a decreasing rate' means).

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{995_q12_s1}

$x$-intercept: put $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}2-\ln x&=0\\ \ln x&=2\\ x&=e^2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $y=2-\ln1=2$. As $x\to0^{+}$, $y\to\infty$, so $x=0$ is a vertical asymptote.

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=5x^4-20x^3\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=20x^3-60x^2\end{aligned}$$
For a point of inflexion, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes:
$$\begin{aligned}20x^3-60x^2&=0\\ 20x^2(x-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=1$, giving $(0,1)$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2920_1}

The concavity does not change, so $(0,1)$ is not a point of inflexion.

When $x=3$, $y=3^5-5(3)^4+1=-161$, giving $(3,-161)$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2920_2}

The concavity changes, so $(3,-161)$ is a point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ \text{the only point of inflexion is }(3,-161)$$

2005.stem:
The predicted number of cases, $C$ of Capona virus strain present in country X, $n$ days after it was first detected is predicted by the model:

$$C=5e^{3n}+1$$

parts.latex: How many cases were present when the virus strain was first detected?
Find the rate at which the number of cases is predicted to be increasing on the 10th day.
State when is the number of cases predicted to first exceed 2 000.

solutions.latex:
When the strain is first detected, $n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}C&=5e^0+1\\ &=6\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 6\text{ cases}$$

The rate of increase is $\dfrac{dC}{dn}$ (cases per day):
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dC}{dn}&=5e^{3n}\cdot3\\ &=15e^{3n}\end{aligned}$$
The first day is $n=0$, so the $10$th day is $n=9$:
$$\dfrac{dC}{dn}=15e^{27}\text{ cases/day}$$

meta.source_flag: 'On the 10th day' is read as $n=9$ (day 1 is $n=0$, as the marking note to part (c) says). If it meant $n=10$ the rate would be $15e^{30}$. Source kept.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}5e^{3n}+1&=2000\\ 5e^{3n}&=1999\\ e^{3n}&=\dfrac{1999}{5}\\ 3n&=\ln\dfrac{1999}{5}\\ n&\approx1.997\end{aligned}$$
The number of cases exceeds $2000$ when $n>1.997$, so this first happens at $n=2$, the $3$rd day.

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: $n$ was given as $1.996$; $\frac{1}{3}\ln\frac{1999}{5}=1.997$. The answer $n=2$ (3rd day) is unchanged.
meta.marker_note: Accept 3rd day or $n=2$. Do not accept the second day, as $n=0$ is the first day.

2006.stem:
A buoy is suspended in the ocean. At its lowest point, the buoy is at a height of 16 metres above the sea floor. At its maximum height, it reaches 28 metres above the sea floor.

The tide mimics a sinusoidal wave, such that one full cycle of the tide going both in and out occurs in 30 hours.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of h(t) cosine curve with levels 28, 22, 16
solution sketch: sketch of h(t) over 60 hours with line at 20 metres and four intersections

parts.latex:
If the buoy is initially at its highest point, show that the buoy follows an equation above sea level of

$$h(t)=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right)+22$$

where $h(t)$ is the height of the buoy above the sea floor in metres after $t$ hours.
State the number of times the buoy reaches a level of 20 metres above the sea floor in the first 60 hours.

If the buoy was at its highest point above the sea floor at 2 a.m on Monday, at what times does the buoy reach 20 metres above the sea floor within the next 60 hours. Leave your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{995_q14_s1}

The buoy moves between $16$ m and $28$ m:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{amplitude}&=\dfrac{28-16}{2}=6\\ \text{rest position}&=28-6=22\end{aligned}$$
One cycle takes $30$ hours, so $n=\dfrac{2\pi}{30}=\dfrac{\pi}{15}$. The buoy starts at its highest point, so the curve is a cosine curve, $h=a\cos(nt)+22$ with $a=6$:
$$h(t)=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{15}\right)+22$$
criteria: At least 1 correct solution for $a$, $n$, or rest position

meta.top_criterion_original: Full correct proof of all terms (cannot award A1 if cosine curve is not stated)
meta.marker_note: The full mark cannot be awarded if the cosine curve is not stated.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}20&=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)+22\\ -2&=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)\\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Let $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{15}t$. For $0\le t\le60$, $0\le\theta\le4\pi$. The acute angle is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3}=1.231$ rad, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\theta&=\pi-1.231,\ \pi+1.231,\ 3\pi-1.231,\ 3\pi+1.231\\ &=1.911,\ 4.373,\ 8.194,\ 10.656\end{aligned}$$
Using $t=\dfrac{15\theta}{\pi}$:
$$t=9\text{ h }7\text{ min},\ 20\text{ h }53\text{ min},\ 39\text{ h }7\text{ min},\ 50\text{ h }53\text{ min}$$
Adding these to $2$ a.m. Monday, the buoy is at $20$ m at
$$\begin{aligned}&11{:}07\text{ am Monday}\\ &10{:}53\text{ pm Monday}\\ &5{:}07\text{ pm Tuesday}\\ &4{:}53\text{ am Wednesday}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: To simplify equation and arrive at $-\dfrac{1}{3}=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the third value of $\frac{\pi}{15}t$ was printed as $3.1937$; it is $3\pi-1.231=8.194$ (the time 39 h 7 min was already right).
meta.marker_note: Accept 24-hour times: 11:07, 22:53, 17:07 (Tuesday), 04:53 (Wednesday).

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle is given by the equation below, where $t$ is the time in seconds for $0\le t\le 9$

$$x=\dfrac{t^3}{3}-4t^2+12t-2$$

Find the time(s) when the particle is at rest.

For the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1+x}{e^{x}}$, $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\infty$ .

Sketch $y=f(x)$ showing all key features including any stationary points and points of inflexion.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=t^2-8t+12\\ t^2-8t+12&=0\\ (t-2)(t-6)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=2\text{ s or }t=6\text{ s}$$

\exfigure{995_q15_s1}

$f(x)=e^{-x}(1+x)$. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-x} & v&=1+x\\ u'&=-e^{-x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=-e^{-x}(1+x)+e^{-x}\\ &=e^{-x}\left(1-(1+x)\right)\\ &=-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$: $-xe^{-x}=0$ gives $x=0$, since $e^{-x}\ne0$. Then $f(0)=\dfrac{1+0}{e^0}=1$, giving $(0,1)$.

To find the nature, differentiate $f'(x)=-xe^{-x}$ with the product rule, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=-e^{-x}+(-x)\left(-e^{-x}\right)\\ &=e^{-x}(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$f''(0)=e^0(-1)=-1<0$, so $(0,1)$ is a local maximum.

For points of inflexion, $f''(x)=0$: $e^{-x}(x-1)=0$ gives $x=1$, since $e^{-x}\ne0$. Then $f(1)=\dfrac{2}{e}$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2928_1}

$f''(0)=-1<0$ and $f''(2)=e^{-2}(2-1)=\dfrac{1}{e^2}>0$, so the concavity changes and $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.

As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to0$, so the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.
criteria: Determines POI (not awarded if concavity change not tested)
Determines nature of stationary point through $f''(x)$ and sub $x$ value
Attempts differentiation using product or quotient rule

Max (0,1), POI (1,2/e) and x-intercept -1 are at their true positions on that curve (rules 16, 18); ticks at -1, 1, 2 on one even scale (rule 17).
